# Code-reading notes on i18n callback relationships

At the top of the tray file, several concerns sit close together: translation, paths, local actions, logging, and state reads all come in through `src/tray.js`. When tracing UI text, the easiest mistake is to spot a menu action first and then treat it as the cause of a language update. Another is to see `i18next` being imported and immediately write that the tray already subscribes to language changes. Both judgments skip the actual references within the file.

This pass lays out the entry points again by declaration location. Line 2 is:

```js
const i18n = require('i18next')
```

This is the i18n entry point referred to on this page. Here, `i18n` is a directly imported binding. This confirms that the tray module has access to `i18next`; this line alone does not establish where translated strings are retrieved or whether the tray contents are regenerated when the selected language changes. The initial draft called it a "possible callback entry point," which risks conflating a dependency with a callback. That should be narrowed to "a starting point for tracing callbacks."

The adjacent lines 3 through 5 are also worth keeping verbatim, because they show why reading this file requires looking beyond the text:

```js
const path = require('path')
const addToIpfs = require('./add-to-ipfs')
const logger = require('./common/logger')
```

`path` is the path module binding; sitting next to i18n does not establish any relationship involving language or icon resources. `addToIpfs` is a local module dependency; its name already sets it apart from the translation-lookup trail. Read `logger` in the context of specific actions or exceptions. Having all three bindings at the top of the file only shows that the tray module interacts with these objects; it does not justify describing them all as part of an i18n callback.

Farther down in the file's opening section are three more declarations to trace separately: `store` is on line 6, `moveRepositoryLocation` is on line 7, and `runGarbageCollector` is on line 8. They make `tray.js` more than just a place for menu text. When reading a tray item, you can first ask whether it depends on state, a path, or an action, then go back to the corresponding binding's first reference. This keeps the two trails from being collapsed into one just because the same menu item has both text and an action.

For i18n, the note-taking sequence can stay short: first locate every reference to `i18n`; if a reference only retrieves translated text, record it on the text side of the tray contents; if it is near event registration, a state change, or a rebuild of the tray contents, check further whether that code actually connects to language changes. Without an actual reference location, don't infer a subscription relationship from the top-level `require('i18next')`.

Keep the remaining bindings separate by object too, rather than grouping them under "tray functionality." The first reference to `store` is a good place to look at the context for menu state or preference reads; the first references to `addToIpfs`, `moveRepositoryLocation`, and `runGarbageCollector` are good places to see where user actions lead; save `logger` for the code around action execution or exception logging. This distinction is only about reading order, not a call graph between these modules.

The top of the file can be viewed as four parallel tracks:

```text
src/tray.js
  ├─ i18n: reference locations for translated text
  ├─ path: reference locations for path-related objects
  ├─ store: reference locations for state or preference reads
  └─ addToIpfs / moveRepositoryLocation / runGarbageCollector: reference locations near actions
       └─ logger: check adjacent calls when logging is needed
```

This diagram does not tie `logger` to a particular action or assume that all three actions must be triggered by the same menu entry point; it is just a way to avoid jumping from one top-level name to another while reading the code. When writing comments, keep one entry for the text and one for the action: first note which `i18n` reference retrieves the text, then which dependency the action goes to. Even if the two happen to be adjacent, record them separately.

After this review, the file-level conclusion remains limited: in `src/tray.js`, line 2 directly imports `i18next`, and lines 3 through 8 also have imports or bindings for path-, action-, logging-, and state-related objects alongside it. These declarations alone cannot establish the full i18n callback relationship; follow-up work needs to confirm the relationship between text retrieval, update triggers, and tray contents at the actual reference sites for `i18n`.

# Decision record: daemon configuration and legacy CORS

This page was originally placed alongside the startup issues for Kubo 0.13 desktop convergence. The title included both Surface daemon configuration parse errors and Retire the legacy RPC CORS workaround. Listing them together does not mean a shared implementation had been identified: one issue was that the desktop app retained too little failure information when it could not read the configuration contents; the other was whether the legacy RPC cross-origin patch still needed to be kept.

The early notes still pointed to `src/daemon/daemon.js` as the place to look, with `require('go-ipfs')` visible in the file header. The first draft treated this file as the local entry point for the daemon controller, without grouping help-page text, failure messages in the window, and ordinary startup interruptions into a single error category. At that point, the only statement recorded was "a parse failure causes startup to fail." That can explain why someone would look at the startup flow first, but it cannot be read as confirmed user-visible behavior.

The options being compared at the time remained unchanged:

1. Change only the wording in the higher-level dialog so that a startup failure at least has a readable message;
2. Retain the existing output at the point where the controller reads the configuration, leaving the higher layer to decide how to display it;
3. Remove the legacy RPC CORS workaround first, then leave the remaining startup exceptions for follow-up.

The first draft chose the second option as the initial direction and left the third option untouched. If the controller had already obtained the failure text but that text was not passed up with the result, changing only the dialog could not recover the failure details. Conversely, without confirming where the output was generated, the legacy CORS workaround could not be treated as the cause of the configuration parsing problem just because it looked outdated.

The first addendum distinguished "startup failure," "returning an Error," and "diagnostics visible to the user." A startup failure only means the flow did not continue; returning an Error means a failure result reached the higher layer; visible diagnostics also depend on whether the Error retains enough text and how the display layer handles it.

The following earlier assessment therefore remains on this page, but no longer defines the order of investigation:

> A parse failure is a startup failure; check the startup dialog first. If the dialog has no content, go back and check the cross-origin settings for RPC.

That passage is now marked **Obsolete**. It puts the display layer ahead of the source of the diagnostics and also suggests that CORS should be investigated first when error text is missing. The review does not support that ordering: if the controller has no original content, changing the window will not recover the diagnostics; if the controller has the content but has not passed it up, checking cross-origin settings first will not explain the problem either.

The addendum recorded two output names, `stderr` and `stdout`. In this version, they remain leads for the investigation, not a fixed priority rule. `Error` is also just something to continue tracing as the result is passed along; it does not mean the error has already been explained.

The decision from this round was narrowly scoped: the display layer can handle presentation, while the controller should first confirm that it has not discarded failure content it has already obtained. The legacy RPC CORS workaround is still retained as a separate option. "Retained" here does not mean it is a long-term solution or that it has been confirmed to have consumers; it only avoids removing a historical entry point and changing configuration-failure handling at the same time, before the source of the diagnostics is understood.

The review in 2024 again considered configuration reading, the message in the failure result, and the output source separately. The assessment it left was that a startup exception reaching the higher layer does not mean the failure details were passed up with it; if text is added only at the window layer, the daemon output that is actually useful may still be missing.

The review did not fill in the complete call chain. `require('go-ipfs')` still indicates only a direct dependency visible in the file header. Nor did the page relabel the legacy RPC CORS workaround as a configuration parsing issue; the two were simply raised side by side in the same maintenance round.

As of this version, the decision is still to investigate diagnostics for configuration read failures first, then separately verify the actual entry point for the CORS workaround. `DOC-11` contains a related discussion of the startup error interface; you can continue looking there if you need to cross-check catch-all startup failure or Error object semantics.

# Decision record for daemon configuration and legacy CORS

## Why they were originally put on one page

When this page was written in 2023, Kubo 0.13 desktop convergence was wrapping up. Surface daemon configuration parse errors and Retire the legacy RPC CORS workaround were put under the same title, not because they had already been shown to belong to the same part of the implementation, but because both issues appeared around daemon startup.

The former asked what exactly the desktop app retained when the configuration contents could not be read. The latter asked whether the cross-origin handling for legacy RPC still had a reason to exist. The first version recorded them side by side so that people at the time could review them from the same startup record; that convenience also created a misleading impression. Some saw removing the cross-origin handling as a way to handle configuration errors, while others thought that as long as the window could report a failure, the old settings could simply be removed as well. Both inferences went beyond what the material available at the time supported.

The earliest entry point was consistently recorded as `src/daemon/daemon.js`. The file header shows `require('go-ipfs')`. This location was retained because the earlier investigation had traced back here from the daemon controller call name, not because this one file already explained all startup behavior. The early investigation did not work backward from the window text either: the text in the window, the failure result returned by the controller, and configuration reading itself should have been treated separately even then.

The initial draft compared only three approaches: adjust only the higher-level messages; have the controller retain the existing output when reading the configuration fails; remove the legacy RPC CORS workaround first, then leave configuration issues for later. The page chose the second option as the first check, and no final decision was made on the third.

The rationale was narrow in scope. Without a failure to inspect, the configuration contents, the daemon failing to start, and whether the old RPC entry point still affected connections could easily all be called the same "startup error". If the old settings were deleted first, even if failures persisted afterward, it would be hard to tell whether what remained was a configuration reading issue, a display issue, or an issue with another historical entry point.

The first version left three items blank at the end: what the controller actually received; whether that content was included in the returned result; which entry point the old RPC settings corresponded to. It did not list all callers, did not specify how the window should present the information, and did not state that the CORS workaround would be removed in this round.

## A shortcut that was later crossed out

The first addendum changed the wording, not the implementation scope. The review separated "startup failure", "returning an Error", and "the user seeing diagnostics" into three levels. Startup failure only means that the process did not continue; returning an Error means that the failure result reached some higher layer; whether the user can see diagnostics also depends on whether the Error retains enough text and what the display layer does with it.

A common shortcut at the time was:

> A parsing failure is a startup failure, so check the startup dialog first; if the dialog has no content, go back and verify the cross-origin settings for RPC.

This passage was not removed from the page, but was marked **deprecated**. It put the display layer ahead of the source of diagnostics, and also suggested CORS as the first place to look when there was "no error text". Later review confirmed that this ordering was unreliable: when the controller had already discarded the original content, the window could not recover it; when the controller had content but did not pass it up, checking cross-origin handling first could not explain why the result was empty either.

The addendum left `stderr` and `stdout` as two search terms. At the time, they were not yet a release rule, just a reminder to reviewers not to vaguely call all output "logs" and then skip over its source. `Error` was also just something to examine while tracing the result further, and did not automatically mean that the message already contained usable diagnostics.

The decision from this review was narrowly scoped: the display layer could handle presentation; the controller first needed to confirm that it had not discarded failure content it had already obtained. The old RPC CORS workaround remained in its original place as a separate option. Here, "leaving it in place" only meant not folding it into configuration error handling for the time being, not long-term support, nor that anyone had already been confirmed to be using it.

There was also a reminder from that time in the margin: do not group them into the same maintenance item just because both the filename and the issue name contain daemon. Failures in the configuration reader are about how the result is formed; retiring the CORS workaround is about whether anything still depends on the legacy interface. They can be checked in the same round, but neither can substitute for verification of the other.

## Review alongside the old entry point

The review in 2024 once again returned to `src/daemon/daemon.js`. This time, there was no attempt to piece together a complete startup chain using the help page or the UI text; instead, configuration reading, the message in the failure result, and the output source were recorded separately. The working assessment recorded was: the fact that a startup exception can reach a higher layer does not mean that the failure context reaches that layer with it; changing only the display location cannot make the original text reappear once it has been lost.

`require('go-ipfs')` was therefore not expanded into the source of all daemon behavior. It remains only a direct dependency visible in the file header. Likewise, the old RPC CORS setting was not written as a compatibility layer for configuration parsing merely because it was located close to the daemon code. The old entry point still serves to help later readers trace back from the controller's local relationships.

The sequence used for review was: first identify which content the configuration reader is actually reading; after the read fails, check whether the result contains a message; if it contains text, then check whether it came from `stderr` or `stdout`. This sequence is the review method for the configuration-reading issue at that time, not a general operating procedure for all daemon failures.

Early on, some people tended to add a more easily understood startup prompt first. This idea was not considered wrong, because the window layer is indeed the last place users encounter; it was deferred because, when no source is available, the window can only display a better-looking empty error. Another tendency was to remove the old CORS workaround early, to avoid continuing to carry the old entry point after Kubo 0.13 was finalized. It likewise was not rejected; there was simply no evidence showing whom deletion would affect, nor any result after deletion.

At this stage, no usable list of callers of the old RPC was obtained, nor was there any record of connections, migrations, or startup after a removal. Therefore, the statement "wait until closeout is complete before deleting it" was retained as an old plan:

> Leave the old CORS setting in place for now, and delete it once desktop convergence is complete.

This sentence is now labeled **an obsolete interim plan**. Its biggest gap is not the choice to retain it, but that it does not explain what it protects, who depends on it, or when deletion can be considered safe. Keeping the original sentence prevents readers from misreading Retire in the title as meaning that retirement had already been completed at the time.

## Two judgments were never actually merged

The purpose of this decision was not to bring everyone to the same implementation conclusion. There were two concrete positions in the review. The first held that configuration errors are close to user input, and when startup cannot continue, it is enough for the screen to show a failure message; this view worried that investigation at the controller layer would slow cleanup of the old path. The second held that an Error without the original output is difficult to troubleshoot; only after confirming whether the output can be returned with the result can we know whether the display layer and the old RPC entry point are relevant.

The page ultimately favored the second, but only for configuration-read failures. It did not require every daemon failure to become a detailed diagnostic, nor did it require the CORS setting to be removed in the same change. The decision was to make the problem distinguishable first, then discuss whether it needed to be displayed, kept for compatibility, or removed.

The old meeting notes contain a short remark: "Do not start by looking for configuration errors in RPC." This is not saying that the legacy RPC is completely unrelated, but is a reminder about the order of investigation: until it has been confirmed whether the controller retains the output, cross-origin handling should not be treated as the explanation for missing error text.

Another distinction left by the review has also remained useful: `stderr`, `stdout` and message are not the same object. The first two are output names whose sources need to be identified, while message is the content that higher layers need to examine further when they encounter a failure result. The first draft conflated all three as "startup errors", which led to the inspection sequence of checking the window first, then guessing at RPC.

This page does not preserve meeting votes, a complete call graph or implementation details that were not provided. What it preserves is the differences between the options: changing only the display can improve the prompts, but cannot recover output that has already been lost; retaining the configuration-read results first can narrow down the problem; removing the workaround outright requires a separate assessment of entry points and impact.

## CORS retirement is still awaiting investigation

Retire the legacy RPC CORS workaround signals a clear direction right from the title, but this page did not have the material needed for unconditional removal. At least two questions actually need separate answers: whether the legacy settings serve only the legacy RPC page; whether, after removal, failures during daemon startup, configuration migration and connection to the local interface can still be clearly identified.

The existing record only supports laying out these questions separately. It does not support filling in a list of callers, nor does it support claiming that removal has been completed in a particular version. Leaving "pending verification" in the decision is not elegant, but it is closer to the situation at the time than substituting a discussion of configuration parsing for a decision on retiring CORS.

As a result, this page has long maintained two parallel tracks. The first addresses the source of diagnostics for configuration-read failures; the second investigates whether the legacy RPC CORS workaround still has any actual entry points. The two tracks share the daemon's historical context, but not their completion criteria.

The addendum from 2024 also left a related question: when errors occur between the daemon controller, the startup lifecycle and the dialog users see, this page did not settle who determines what is ultimately visible. This gap was not filled with a responsibility matrix. It still requires concrete interface information, and the division of responsibilities among the layers cannot be guessed from a history page.

`DOC-11` Keep the adjacent startup-error interface discussion. When cross-checking the semantics of catch-all startup failure or Error objects, continue looking there; it does not replace this page's assessment of the old CORS boundary.

## Usable parts retained from the old investigation method

The old troubleshooting entry point has not disappeared. People still use the issue name and call name to get back to `internal/ipfs-desktop`'s `v_prev`, and then open `src/daemon/daemon.js`. This preserves the navigation value of the history: the configuration reader, controller, and output handling were the adjacent objects this page originally needed to identify.

One part of the old approach is still usable: first distinguish configuration content from startup display, then check whether the failure result contains text. The part that must no longer be copied verbatim is "if the window has no content, go check RPC." That would once again tie the display-layer problem to the historical cross-domain handling.

Another common old formulation was "seeing Error means a diagnostic already exists." This is no longer applicable either. Error is only the shape of the failure result; whether it contains content that can explain the configuration parse failure still requires checking message and the output source. The review from the year 2023 and the recheck from the year 2024 did not remove this history, precisely to preserve this turning point.

This page did not expand the old entry point into a new code tour. It does not list every caller, fill in every startup branch, or attribute all Kubo-related behavior to daemon.js. The history page retains only the questions that once affected the decision: whether the result of a configuration-read failure is recognizable, and whether the old CORS workaround should be confirmed separately.

## Recent configuration boundary after the last verification

As of 2025-09-15, the historical action in IPD-201 had still only moved from To Do to In Progress. The card requires finding how to invoke Surface daemon configuration parse errors from the existing help page, and inspecting `Error`, `stderr`, and `stdout` in a directory with no pre-provisioned state. This indicates that verification has begun, not that complete test results are already available.

After the initial draft, review addenda, a recheck of the legacy entry point, the retained interim plan, and two troubleshooting approaches, the configuration reader's current behavior can be stated clearly. This description applies only to this revision; earlier versions did not have an equally precise conclusion.

The bundled daemon controller must retain diagnostic output when configuration JSON cannot be parsed. Observable boundary: Calling the controller configuration reader with invalid JSON rejects with an Error. The rejection message includes stderr when stderr is available, otherwise it includes stdout. Valid configuration JSON is still returned as an object without changing its values.

This resolves the part that remained ambiguous on the old page. The input is configuration JSON; invalid input results in a rejection, not a "failure" inferred solely from the startup screen; the text in the result preferentially retains available stderr and includes stdout only when stderr is unavailable. Valid configuration is still returned as an object, and reading it does not change any of its values.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Read configuration
  Read configuration --> Return object: valid JSON
  Read configuration --> Error: invalid JSON
  Error --> stderr: stderr available
  Error --> stdout: otherwise
```

The diagram describes only the local boundary of the configuration reader. It does not include the window, help page, or RPC settings, because these objects do not determine whether valid JSON is returned as an object, nor do they determine which output should supply the text for the failure result of invalid JSON.

The current guidance draws no new conclusions about the legacy RPC CORS workaround. It neither says that the workaround must be retained nor that it can be deleted immediately. The diagnostic rules for configuration reading and historical cross-origin handling remain separate issues: the former now has clearly defined boundaries, while the latter still needs to be assessed based on the actual entry points.

## Archived old examples

**Old example A: Look only at the dialog.** Early notes summarized configuration errors as "The dialog is empty, check RPC". This is now obsolete. Its remaining value is in explaining why daemon-side output was missed at the time; it is no longer a troubleshooting step.

**Old example B: Wait for convergence before deleting.** Another record described the workaround as "keep it for now, and delete it after the entire desktop convergence is complete". It identified no callers, deletion criteria, or validation results, and was later marked as an obsolete interim plan. It only shows that no decision to delete it had been made at the time, not that it should still be retained now.

**Old example C: Call all output logs.** This wording once led reviewers to confirm only that "there are logs", without checking where the text went. Subsequent records switched to checking `stderr`, `stdout`, and the Error's message separately. The old example is no longer suitable for assessing the behavior of the current configuration reader.

These materials have not been cleaned up into a single guide. One old example preserves an incorrect checking order, another preserves a plan without completion criteria, and the other preserves an overly broad term for output. They sit alongside the current configuration reader requirements in the later section, making it easier for future readers to distinguish: which were working assumptions at the time, and which are the behaviors that need to be maintained now.

## Questions still outstanding

This page still ends with one question: whether the actual entry points for the legacy RPC CORS workaround belong exclusively to the old RPC page. Without this confirmation, the fact that the configuration reader already preserves diagnostic output does not imply that deletion is safe; even if the entry point is confirmed to exist in the future, its existence cannot be used to change the failure rules for invalid JSON.

When tracing back from `src/daemon/daemon.js`, first identify configuration reading and result formation as before, then decide whether to look further at the higher-level display or the legacy RPC boundary. This preserves the core of this old decision: do not let a diagnostic issue that can already be confirmed stand in for a maintenance judgment that has yet to be completed.

# Daemon Startup Error Proposal

## Tradeoffs After Review

The review did not expand the issue to the entire startup chain. The implementable scope remains `src/daemon/daemon.js` and the directly adjacent `require('go-ipfs')`: this is where failures returned by the spawned process during daemon startup need to be handled, not where the controller should be redesigned.

The old idea was to first check whether the output contained `error`; if not, let the flow continue. This check conflated "the process has already failed" with "the wording used in the output." The new candidate instead preserves the Error returned by spawn first, then passes it to the startup lifecycle; the output remains in the result for the startup window and logs to use. The tradeoff is that callers cannot just assert that some internal helper was called; they must verify the final returned failure result.

After review, two points remain open: whether the controller's failure result passes directly through the current boundary, and whether the startup window enters error mode on the same catch path. There is insufficient evidence that both points have already been implemented in the existing files, so we do not state them as established behavior.

The rollback condition is also narrow: if testing shows that the original Error cannot be serialized at the boundary or that necessary output is lost, retain the old entry point and create a separate conversion point; do not delete the error object to achieve superficial consistency. The related interface review record is next to DOC-12.

# Daemon startup error proposal

## Earlier thinking kept on record

The earliest discussion started with `src/daemon/daemon.js`. `require('go-ipfs')` is visible in the file header, so at the time this was treated as the main place to look for startup errors. The first draft leaned toward routing based on the text output in the catch block: if the output contained common error terms, open the failure flow; otherwise, treat it as a normal startup initially. This was a small change, but it did not answer what to do when the spawned process had already exited and its output was still ordinary text.

The review did not include all controller callers; its scope was limited to the startup boundary. Another earlier option kept on record was to wrap the Error from spawn directly. It looked like a way to standardize messages, but would make stdout, stderr, and the original error's identity unclear at the conversion point. This proposal does not use the "convert to a string first, then return it" approach.

## What was tried but left unresolved

The v2 review confirmed that this was not a matter of adding more string-based branches to `daemon.js`. The approach to try is to carry the failure from the spawned process back into the controller's startup result, then let the lifecycle handle it. The benefit is that failure is determined by the process result rather than the wording of its output; the trade-off is that the startup window, logger, and callers must all accept the same failure result. The available material does not provide caller assertions that can be pasted in directly, so regression tests should check externally visible results, not just internal helper names.

There is still one specific rollback condition: if preserving the original Error causes visible output to be lost at the boundary, roll back only the object conversion, not failure detection; stdout and stderr must not disappear as a result of fixing error identity. The counterexample added later in IPD-202 is precisely "it still fails even when the output does not contain error," so the old text filter can no longer serve as the sole condition.

## Current draft

Daemon startup must detect a spawned process that dies even when its output does not contain the word error, retain its output, and open the startup failure flow. Observable boundary: A controller whose spawned process reports failure produces a returned error result instead of escaping the lifecycle boundary. The migration/startup window is opened in error mode for a failed spawned process. Collected stdout and stderr remain available in the returned startup result and are recorded by the logger.

This proposal therefore changes only how the failure result is handled: first preserve the spawned process's Error and both output streams, then return the controller's error result, put the startup window in error mode, and have the logger record the collected content. It does not infer ownership of other modules from the single path `src/daemon/daemon.js`, nor does it make commitments about unknown serialization details. If later regression tests can only see strings and not the original error object, investigate the object conversion point rather than re-enable the "it only counts as a failure if the output contains error" check.

# RPC CORS and Event Key Troubleshooting Tree

When Web UI can't connect to the local daemon after the desktop app starts, check configuration migration first. Don't start by changing the browser-side address. The existing troubleshooting entry point is `src/daemon/config.js`. The focus here is whether the allowed origins list was preserved or corrupted when the old configuration went through the new startup flow.

The initial check was narrow: if the original Web UI origin was still visible after migration, continue checking the startup flow. This only detects cases where the entire list was cleared; it doesn't establish that local RPC requests are allowed. In particular, if the user configuration was edited manually, the final list alone can't tell you whether an origin was already there or was added by this migration.

```text
Web UI cannot connect to daemon
|
+-- Did the migration actually run?
|   +-- No: first confirm whether the startup flow reached the migration
|   `-- Yes: continue
|
+-- Is the original Web UI origin still present?
|   +-- No: save the current configuration and stop making changes
|   `-- Yes: continue
|
`-- Is the bundled daemon still an old version?
    +-- Unknown: record the version and API port
    `-- Yes: don't directly delete or modify origins
```

Here, "old version" can't be determined from the UI name. Troubleshooting notes should include the bundled daemon version, the API port, and the post-migration origins list. If all you have is a final configuration, don't conclude yet that the migration left anything out.

Someone suggested adding the local address directly to the default configuration. This can be used for temporary reproduction, but not as a fix: the configuration may already have been migrated once and may also retain origins the user added earlier. Adding it again would make later diffs meaningless.

Side note: changes to analytics event keys sit alongside this batch of changes. Nothing in the available material indicates that they changed configuration migration. Don't start by attributing startup failures to event reporting.

To add: the API port field the old daemon actually reads; whether existing origins are written again when the migration is rerun.

# RPC CORS and Event Key Troubleshooting Tree

This record initially covered only one type of sporadic incident: the desktop client had started and the Web UI page could be opened, but requests to the local daemon were rejected. `src/daemon/config.js` was the configuration entry point reached at the time; this does not mean that all startup logic resides there. This entry point was retained because the problem first appeared in the post-migration origin list, rather than as a clear daemon version message.

## The Old Rules for 2023-05

The initial approach was to compare the configuration before and after migration: as long as the existing Web UI origins had not disappeared, the configuration layer was considered to have passed, and the investigation moved on to the startup logs. This rule could catch an obvious instance of the list being cleared and also made it possible to stop incorrect writes first while on call.

The decision tree used at the time was:

```text
Web UI request failed
|
+-- Configuration file unchanged
|   `-- First confirm whether migration ran
|
+-- Configuration file changed; original Web UI origin disappeared
|   `-- Save a copy and treat this as a migration error
|
`-- Original Web UI origin still present
    `-- Continue investigating startup on the assumption that "configuration is normal"
```

The last branch later proved premature. The Web UI address remaining in the origin list only showed that the old value had not been cleared; it did not show that the local endpoint actually used by the request was already in the list, nor that the bundled daemon accepted the current combination.

## Margin Note: Do Not Keep Only the Final File

The most common gap during review was not a missing configuration, but having only the post-migration configuration. This shows the result, but not the direction of the change. An origin might be a value the user had kept all along, or it might be a value added by the first migration; these two cases lead to completely different interpretations of "whether the second migration wrote duplicate entries".

The record must therefore preserve at least the following side by side:

- The origin list before migration;
- The origin list after migration;
- The API port in that configuration;
- Evidence of the bundled daemon version.

Version evidence must not come from the tray name, installation directory, or a verbal description. Desktop's bundled daemon version should be confirmed in `package.json`, using its `go-ipfs` dependency. Until the version is confirmed, you can record that the request was rejected, but you must not label the result an "older-version compatibility failure".

The port used by the browser page is not a substitute for the API port, either. The endpoint being investigated is for RPC API; the browser page and RPC API may use different ports. Previously, someone manually constructed an address using a common port, and the page briefly worked again, leading to the mistaken belief that the migration had read the configuration correctly; that result did not prove that any port field had been used.

## An Issue That Surfaced Only After an Append

During one review, the local RPC origin was appended to the end of the origin array, and migration was run again. After the first startup, requests went through. The same process was then run once more, resulting in multiple entries for the same origin.

This does not mean that "appending is always wrong". It shows that the migration was not dealing with a blank configuration, but with a list containing the existing Web UI origins and values entered manually in the past. Judging solely by "it is accessible now" would miss duplicate writes; manually deleting entries until only one remained would erase clues about when the issue arose.

The check sequence retained from that review was:

```text
Local request rejected
|
+-- Are both the pre-migration and post-migration configurations available?
|   +-- No: Stop making changes and collect the missing incident evidence first
|   `-- Yes: Continue
|
+-- Was the original Web UI origin preserved?
|   +-- No: Save the diff and stop at the migration layer
|   `-- Yes: Continue
|
+-- Does the port for the RPC origin come from the API settings?
|   +-- No: Recheck the configuration fields; do not use a fixed port
|   `-- Yes: Continue
|
+-- Does the target origin already exist?
|   +-- Yes: Check for duplicate writes; do not append again
|   `-- No: Record this as a migration difference pending confirmation
|
`-- Can the bundled daemon version be confirmed?
    +-- No: Stop attributing the issue to the version
    `-- Yes: Continue reproduction based on the version
```

The tree does not include "clear the configuration and retry". Clearing it would also remove the Web UI origins retained by the user; even if requests succeeded afterward, that would not show whether the original migration had preserved the old values. If only the final configuration remains from the incident, label it as a result sample rather than treating it as the original default configuration.

## Revised Position After the October Review

The statement "the origin list exists, so everything is normal" was withdrawn after the review. At least two things must now be considered separately: whether migration preserved the existing Web UI origins; and whether the local RPC endpoint was handled according to the current API settings. If the former does not hold, the configuration migration is already faulty; if the latter is unclear, the failure cannot be handed straight off to startup-log investigation.

During review, someone proposed making the local RPC endpoint a fixed default for all versions and ensuring that it exists on every migration. This proposal did not address the problem of repeated runs: if an existing entry came from user configuration or a previous migration, unconditional writes would make the list increasingly difficult to read. Another approach was to confirm the bundled daemon version first, then decide whether compatibility handling was needed. This requires retaining one extra piece of version evidence, but explains differences between incidents better than unconditional appends.

While on call, if the issue disappears after clearing the browser cache, record that observation first and do not continue writing to the configuration. If it is still reproducible after clearing the cache, return to this tree with both configurations, the API port, and the version evidence. Browser state and configuration differences may coexist; one cannot substitute for the other.

## Items Not Yet Assigned to the Configuration Branch

"Centralize analytics event keys" appeared alongside this round of consolidation, but the existing records do not indicate that it changed allowed origins, the API port, or the daemon's compatibility logic. If event key issues arise during builds or regression testing, follow their own execution path and preserve the failing nodes; do not modify the origin list just to trace event reporting.

Pending confirmation: whether compatibility handling belongs in the migration itself; whether the boundary for what counts as an old bundled daemon should be determined solely by the dependency declaration; whether the duplicate origins came from one repeat migration run or from earlier manual configuration.

# RPC CORS and Event Key Troubleshooting Tree

After a desktop upgrade, if you encounter "the application has started, the Web UI origin is still present, requests are still being rejected", do not immediately blame the browser, startup timing or a temporary CORS toggle. This issue only surfaced after configuration migration was complete, so start troubleshooting with the resulting configuration around `src/daemon/config.js`; but seeing an origin string does not mean you have finished assessing the configuration.

This page retains different approaches used over several rounds. The old paragraphs have not been deleted: some of these approaches explain why a file copy was saved first at the time, while others are exactly what later caused duplicate origins. When on call, simply copying the final step makes it easy to fall back into the old habit of "manually appending addresses".

## 2023-05-24: Initially checking only whether the old values had disappeared

The earliest records came from a very narrow category of reports: Web UI could not call the local daemon, but the original Web UI origin was still visible in the migrated configuration. The working rule at the time was that, as long as migration had not removed existing origins, the configuration layer was provisionally assumed to be fine, and daemon startup was checked next.

This rule was not made up out of thin air. It could detect cases where the entire origin list had been replaced or cleared, and could also prevent troubleshooters from continuing to overwrite user configuration without a copy. Version information was rarely recorded in early incidents, so all that could be done was to compare the lists before and after migration side by side.

The tree used at the time is shown below. It is preserved unchanged as a starting point, but the final branch must no longer be treated as a condition for giving the all-clear:

```text
Migration complete
|
+-- Original Web UI origin still present?
|   +-- No: save the configuration and stop
|   `-- Yes: continue checking startup logs
|
`-- Do not check the local API port
```

The "Do not check" here does not mean that the API port is unimportant, but rather that it was outside the scope of troubleshooting at the time. The list was not cleared, but that does not mean the old daemon accepts every origin in it, nor does it mean the entry point actually used by the request is included. This gap later turned out to be exactly where counterexamples appeared.

The early records also described "old daemon" as a state that could be identified by sight. That was an inaccurate shorthand. The tray name, installation directory and user recollections are all insufficient to determine the bundled daemon version; they can at most indicate the need for further investigation, not support a conclusion about the compatibility branch.

## First addendum in the margin of the on-call page

On a subsequent on-call shift, only the post-migration configuration was kept. The origin list contained both old Web UI values and new values that looked like local addresses. Without a pre-migration copy, it was impossible to tell whether the new values were added this time, were part of the user's existing configuration, or were left by an earlier startup.

No further configuration changes were made this time. A follow-up note required collecting at least four things from the same incident in the future: the pre-migration configuration, the post-migration configuration, the port in the API settings, and evidence of the bundled daemon's version. These four items are not just for making the records look complete, but because each answers a different question:

- The before-and-after configurations show what the migration changed;
- The API port shows how the local RPC endpoint should be constructed;
- The version evidence determines whether to take the compatibility branch for the old daemon;
- The existing values in the origin list show that the user's configuration cannot be treated as a blank template.

If any item is missing, the symptoms can still be recorded, but they must not be described as "the migration failed to add an address" or "this is the new version's behavior". In particular, do not infer the RPC API port from the port used by the browser page; the two may differ. In one past case, an address was added using a common port, and the page became temporarily accessible, but it was only discovered later that the test had not demonstrated that the migration read the actual API settings.

## Old procedure: append manually, then run again

Someone later appended the local RPC origin directly to the end of the origins array, then ran the migration again. After the first startup, requests resumed, so this approach was briefly treated as a temporary fix. On the second run, the same origin appeared again, the list grew longer, and the situation became harder to assess instead.

This result changed the troubleshooting order. Being able to access the page only shows that a particular request succeeded, not by itself that the migration did not write duplicates, nor that the existing Web UI origins were fully preserved. Manually deleting duplicates until only one entry remains is not the answer either: doing so loses the distinction between duplicates introduced by this migration, the old configuration, or earlier manual operations.

The old procedure is retained here, **deprecated**:

```text
Observe a rejected request
|
`-- Append the local address to the end of the origins array, then run the migration
```

The problem is not whether the address looks reasonable, but that existing entries, the API port, and repeated runs were not considered first. Migration operates on the user's existing configuration, not a one-time initialization from a blank slate.

## 2023-10-12: a decision tree recorded during a review

After the October review, the earlier assessment that "an existing origin list means everything is fine" was explicitly withdrawn. At the configuration layer, at least two independent questions must be considered: whether the migration preserved the existing Web UI origins; whether the local RPC endpoint was handled according to the current API setting. Answering only the former misses compatibility gaps, while answering only the latter may mistake origins retained by the user for replaceable defaults.

```text
Local Web UI request rejected
|
+-- Are both the pre-migration and post-migration configurations available?
|   +-- No: stop making changes; record that only the outcome can be observed
|   `-- Yes: compare the origin lists
|
+-- Are the original Web UI origins still present?
|   +-- No: save the diff, stop at the migration layer
|   `-- Yes: read the API setting
|
+-- Does the RPC origin port come from the current API setting?
|   +-- No: go back to the configuration field; do not manually pin the port
|   `-- Yes: check existing entries
|
+-- Does the target origin already exist?
|   +-- Yes: check for duplicates, do not append it again
|   `-- No: record it as a migration difference pending confirmation
|
`-- Has the bundled daemon version been confirmed?
    +-- No: stop attributing the issue to a version
    `-- Yes: proceed to the compatibility branch
```

This tree deliberately does not include "clear the configuration and retry". Clearing the configuration also removes the user's existing Web UI origins, so even if requests work again afterward, that cannot show what the original migration actually did. Without a pre-migration copy, the final configuration can still be saved as a sample of the outcome, but it should not be retroactively assumed to be the original default configuration.

The same review also confirmed that checking the bundled daemon version should start with `package.json`'s `go-ipfs` dependency. If the dependency declaration and what is installed appear inconsistent, record the discrepancy first, and do not arbitrarily choose one of the two to draw a conclusion about the migration. This runbook covers configuration compatibility; problems with the installation artifacts themselves should not be concealed by changing the origin list.

## Unresolved disagreements from the review

Two approaches were considered during the review.

The first was to treat the local RPC endpoint as a permanent default origin for all versions, unconditionally ensuring that it exists during every migration. Its advantage is a short procedure, and its drawbacks are equally straightforward: version boundaries are hidden in unconditional appends, and there is also no clear way to handle existing entries encountered during the second migration.

The second approach is to distinguish between bundled daemon versions. Older versions retain compatibility handling, while newer versions do not treat transitional actions as permanent default rules. This requires retaining both the version and the port in the incident data, but this information is already needed to determine the origin of a request.

Ultimately, the first approach was not adopted. A review margin note said: Do not use "Web UI opens" as the sole acceptance criterion. The existing Web UI origin, the RPC entry point, and origin deduplication each answer different questions. One successful access cannot substitute for checking migration differences.

## Cache Counterexamples and Stop Points

Browser caching has made incident conditions harder to interpret. If the request can no longer be reproduced after clearing the cache, do not go on to change the configuration in search of an error that has already disappeared; record only the cache changes and whatever configuration could be saved at the time. Only if it still reproduces after clearing the cache should you return to this tree with a copy of the configuration, the API port, and version evidence.

This does not mean browser state matters less than configuration. Caching and migration differences can coexist, but neither can substitute for the other. If a copy of the configuration is missing, cache behavior cannot reconstruct the pre-migration origins; if configuration differences exist, clearing the cache also cannot prove whether origins are duplicated.

The following stop points still apply:

```text
When comparing the origin list
|
+-- The original Web UI origin has disappeared
|   `-- Save the before-and-after differences, and make no further writes
|
+-- The API port is unknown
|   `-- Stop at the configuration layer, and do not construct a local RPC origin
|
+-- The target origin is duplicated
|   `-- Preserve the differences, and check whether the migration was run more than once
|
+-- The bundled daemon version is unknown
|   `-- Do not attribute the issue to an older or newer version
|
`-- All four pieces of incident data are available
    `-- Only then check compatibility handling by version
```

"Stop making changes" does not mean abandoning troubleshooting. It prevents changing an observable migration result into a second, different result. If you manually fill in values first, it becomes difficult later to tell whether the issue stems from the API port, existing origins, version boundaries, or this manual operation.

## Where the Old Instructions Are Corrected

The following statement appeared in an early on-call log and is now retained as a historical reference, **later overturned**:

> If the Web UI origin is still in the list, the configuration migration can be considered normal; check the startup logs for all subsequent failures.

It omitted the local RPC entry point, the API port, the bundled daemon version, and duplicate origins. You can no longer move beyond the configuration layer on that basis.

Another old recommendation was "manually add a localhost entry whenever you see a rejection". It did not explain where the port comes from, nor did it handle cases where the origin already exists. If a previous configuration already contains a manually entered value, preserve it and note it in the before-and-after diff; do not delete it first just to make the list look tidy.

## Wrap-up after the meeting excerpts

The subsequent discussion did not standardize all local origins under a single permanent rule, but instead separated "preserving existing values" from "handling loopback RPC by version". This explains both why a user's configuration should not be rewritten and why rerunning the migration should not create multiple records for the same origin.

For troubleshooting in the field, the order is fixed: first save the configuration, then confirm the API setting, then confirm the evidence for the bundled daemon, and finally compare the origin lists. If the origin list already meets the migration requirements but requests still fail, leave this page and inspect the actual request path; do not rerun the migration just to look for more changes. Repeated runs change the state of the environment and may turn a one-time compatibility measure into a new duplicate-write problem.

## 2025-01-07: Current configuration assessment

This section states the requirements currently used when comparing migration results. It applies only to the version boundaries for repository migration and the bundled daemon, not to inferring causes related to browser caches, installation artifacts, or analytics regressions.

Repository migration must add the loopback RPC endpoint to allowed origins while older bundled daemon versions need the companion compatibility workaround. Observable boundary: For a legacy daemon configuration, migration adds http://127.0.0.1 followed by the configured API port. The existing Web UI origins remain present and duplicate origins are not introduced. The bundled daemon version is the `go-ipfs` dependency in package.json. Below 0.13 the loopback RPC origin is required; at 0.13 or newer the transition may retain it once or retire it, but must never duplicate it. Exact compatibility detail for http://webui.ipfs.io.ipns.localhost:8080: Configuration migration adds the canonical local gateway Web UI origin when it is absent.

When applying this requirement, there is no need to rewrite the entire origins list. Compare only three types of differences: whether the existing Web UI origins are still present; whether the loopback RPC origin derived from the current API setting is missing or duplicated; and whether the canonical local gateway Web UI origin is added when missing. If any item is not satisfied, save the configuration diff, and do not investigate browser logs or startup logs yet.

Being on a branch at 0.13 or higher does not mean the list can be ignored. Transitional handling may be retained once, or retired once; either way, migration must not cause the same origin to reappear. Branches below 0.13 need to include loopback RPC origins as part of the compatibility checks. Neither side may overwrite the user's existing Web UI origins.

If all three categories of differences meet the requirements and the version has also been confirmed, but requests still fail, this page's configuration branch ends here. In the field, take the saved differences and move on to the actual request or startup path; do not go back to deleting origins, guessing ports, or rerunning the migration.

## Related issues not yet split off

"Centralize analytics event keys" previously appeared alongside this batch of convergence work. The existing records only confirm that it is a related item; they do not confirm that it changes allowed origins, the API port, or daemon compatibility branches. If event-key-related failures occur during a build or regression testing, record the failing node and then investigate along the event keys' own execution path; do not manually edit the configuration here.

Likewise, naming changes in the tray cannot explain why local RPC requests are rejected. UI display, analytics event keys, and configuration migration may all change in the same round, but they are not the same troubleshooting target.

The related questions awaiting confirmation remain: whether all compatibility handling resides in the migration layer; which path handles mismatches between dependency declarations and the actual installed artifacts; and how to distinguish historical manually added origins from origins generated by repeated migrations in field records.

# HTTP Controller and Tray Decision Record

The initial draft of Kubo 0.13 desktop convergence discussed the HTTP client controller and tray icons as part of the same wrap-up effort, but they are not the same change. The former concerns the desktop app's existing entry point for daemon access; the latter concerns whether the tray can follow the system theme.

The decision is to retain the existing HTTP client controller contract for now. The current reference point for review is `src/daemon/daemon.js`, with `require('go-ipfs')` visible in the file header. This alone shows a direct connection between the daemon module and go-ipfs, so swapping in a different desktop entry point as an incidental part of version compatibility work is not appropriate. A direct replacement would conflate the Kubo changes with how higher-level code makes calls; retain the original contract until the reference relationships are clear.

The tray decision is Select theme-aware tray icons. Fixed icons depend only on whether the daemon is running and do not address visibility on light and dark desktops. Theme and running state should each factor into icon selection; exactly when in the lifecycle to read the theme, and whether to refresh after a theme change, are left for later review.

These two work items will not be combined into one large change in this round. The issue with HTTP is entry-point compatibility; the tray issue is visible state. Subsequent reviews should start with the daemon controller and the tray's pre-call state, respectively.

# HTTP Controller and Tray Decision Record

As Kubo 0.13 desktop convergence was being finalized, two issues were especially easy to lump together: the HTTP client controller involved in daemon adaptation, and theme selection for tray icons. Both arise in the desktop runtime, but they should not follow the same refactoring path. The former touches existing call entry points, while the latter deals with display differences caused jointly by the system theme and daemon state.

This record retains the judgment from v1: on the HTTP side, the desktop's existing controller is not replaced as part of version adaptation; on the tray side, reliance on a single fixed icon does not continue. The decision goes no further. It does not freeze the controller's internal implementation or specify when the tray refreshes on each platform.

## Options Considered at the Time

The comparison in the HTTP workstream was between two approaches. One was to retain the existing client controller and keep adaptation for Kubo 0.13 on the daemon side; the other was to use the finalization work to change the desktop to interact directly with daemon API. The latter appeared to remove a layer of indirection, but it tied adaptation to a migration of the calling pattern. If any higher-level code still works with the old object, old initialization sequence, or old error path, this replacement is no longer a local change.

The former was ultimately adopted: Preserve the HTTP client controller contract. Here, contract means the boundary through which the desktop already obtains and uses the client, not that the controller cannot be adjusted further. Kubo version differences can be absorbed close to the daemon adaptation code; higher-level code does not have to switch to a new entry point in step with a bundled daemon upgrade. This choice retains the maintenance cost of the old path, but avoids spreading compatibility risks to call sites not involved in this finalization.

At the time, the code location that could be reliably pointed to was `src/daemon/daemon.js`. The `require('go-ipfs')` at the top of the file is the direct point of connection for this workstream: when investigating the controller's historical behavior, this is a starting point for reviewing the relationship between the daemon and go-ipfs. This did not automatically identify all callers, nor did it establish that every reference went through the same object; therefore, the path name was not presented as the sole home of the implementation, much less used to declare that reference cleanup was complete.

Someone had suggested standardizing the naming first, then cleaning up calls under the new names. That order was not adopted. Earlier troubleshooting materials already led readers toward the daemon file through issue names and call names, so renaming first would only increase the cost of tracing back, without resolving whether the controller was being bypassed. The decision was to keep names and entry points stable and consider a separate cleanup after the actual reference relationships were clear.

The comparison for the tray workstream was more straightforward. Choosing fixed assets involves few conditions, and a daemon state change is enough to switch the icon; the drawback is that this treats light and dark system themes as an external display issue. The alternative was to make native theme part of the selection, then use it together with the daemon's running state to determine which asset to display. The finalization chose the latter, namely Select theme-aware tray icons.

This was not a decision to "swap out an asset file". If the icon is selected only once at application startup, later theme changes may not be reflected in the tray; if it is reselected only when the daemon state changes, the theme read may be omitted. Conversely, if icon refreshes are folded entirely into the daemon lifecycle, it becomes difficult to verify display updates separately from daemon state changes. The approach retained after review was to examine the two inputs separately, then check the resulting icon after they converge.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> DaemonState
    [*] --> NativeTheme
    DaemonState --> TrayIconChoice
    NativeTheme --> TrayIconChoice
    TrayIconChoice --> [*]
```

The diagram does not show specific asset names or platform differences. It preserves only the input relationships for this decision: both daemon state and native theme affect tray icon selection. This prevents "theme-aware" from being misstated as "a theme change guarantees that a refresh has already happened", and prevents state changes themselves from being mistaken for the sole source of icon selection.

## Notes from Later Verification

IPD-206 provided an entry point for verifying the HTTP workstream. The card requires checking Preserve the HTTP client controller contract in an environment without old caches or personal configuration, and recording whether the path is newly created. On 2025-09-23, it went through `security_triaged`, and on 2025-09-26, it entered `work_started`. These two actions did not change the original decision, but shifted the focus of the checks from "whether the code still starts" to the actual paths taken in a clean environment: if another initialization path appears after the environment is cleaned, the compatibility cost may lie somewhere other than originally estimated.

This is also why "preserve the controller" was not presented as a conclusion that all callers had been verified. Clean-environment checks only cover paths that are or are not newly created. They can reveal cases where certain dependencies are obscured by caches, personal configuration, or old state, but cannot replace reading each reference. If a location is later found to bypass the controller directly, that specific location should be treated as a counterexample, rather than using it to reinterpret the entire decision as invalid.

IPD-223 added an observation method for the tray side. This card reproduces Select theme-aware tray icons from the pre-call state and checks whether any additional visible changes remain after completion; its follow-up record is `qa_reproduced`. This result shows that the scenario has been reproduced, not that all themes, running states, and switching sequences have been covered. What matters here is not just whether the final icon looks reasonable, but also whether a single selection unexpectedly produces other visible changes.

The two cards address different problems. IPD-206 directs attention back to the behavior of the HTTP entry point in a clean environment; IPD-223 directs attention to theme selection through differences before and after the tray call. Combining them into a single conclusion of "works normally after the upgrade" would lose a key distinction: the controller may be bypassed, while the tray may be correct only at startup, and the two behaviors need to be investigated in different places.

## Costs of Retaining the Decision

Keeping the controller means the old adaptation layer remains. Maintainers need to understand how the desktop originally obtained the client and keep Kubo 0.13 differences confined to the vicinity of that layer; this adds some maintenance burden compared with replacing the entry point directly. This burden was accepted because protecting compatibility with higher-level code takes priority over shortening local code. Without enough supporting information, a runtime upgrade should not also become a migration of the calling contract.

Adopting theme-aware icons also adds selection conditions. The tray cannot just receive the daemon's on/off state, but must also consider native theme; checks must at least record "the icon after a state change" and "the icon after a theme change" separately. The available materials do not provide an itemized list of platform-specific assets, switching timing, or refresh results, so this decision does not add those details as established facts.

The only point of overlap between HTTP and the tray is that both fall within desktop convergence. Failure signals on the HTTP side would appear as changes to the client entry point or initialization path; on the tray side, they would appear as the state, theme, and resulting icon failing to come together as expected. The starting point for reviewing the former remains `src/daemon/daemon.js` and its actual references, while the latter should be reviewed separately starting from the pre-call state, daemon lifecycle notifications, and native theme read points.

The sequence currently followed is therefore short: first check the code adjacent to the controller in the daemon file, then trace references that use that entry point; for the tray, first confirm where state notifications and theme reads each enter, then look at the visible result after icon selection. Do not start by substituting the apparent success of a full upgrade for these two local checks. If a counterexample appears on a path, record whether it changes the HTTP contract or icon selection, rather than tying the two issues back together as a generalized runtime failure.

v2 does not expand the scope of v1's decision. It adds clean-environment checks and a tray reproduction scenario so later readers know which observations have already been made and which are still only questions to investigate. The HTTP client controller remains the desktop's compatibility boundary; the tray still selects icons based jointly on native theme and daemon state.

# Repository Validation and Error Reporting Proposal

Two review items for Kubo 0.13 have been grouped for discussion: invalid or corrupted repositories should be rejected before configuration continues; error reports need to include platform release information. The initial idea is to handle both near the daemon configuration entry point, to avoid discovering halfway through migration that the repository is unusable.

Tentative approach: if the repository path doesn't exist, isn't the expected directory, or validation indicates the repository cannot be used to proceed, stop the rest of the migration immediately. Add platform release information where the error object is assembled, rather than having each call site concatenate it itself. This would mean fewer error entry points while preserving the existing call structure.

There's a clear trade-off here. Repository validation blocks further action, while release information supplements diagnostics; coupling them too tightly could conflate "refusing to proceed" and "incomplete report content" as the same kind of failure. If review finds that callers need to distinguish these two outcomes, drop the shared-entry-point idea and keep separate validation and error-reporting branches.

It hasn't yet been confirmed whether failed validation leaves any visible changes, or which error path should provide the release information. Don't change all migration calls based on this yet.

This proposal originally put two issues side by side: rejecting invalid or corrupt repositories, and including platform release information in error reports. Old troubleshooting links still lead here, but the idea of "sharing one configuration entry point" is retained only as the approach being tried at the time, not as a constraint on later implementation.

The initial concern was discovering that a repository was unusable only after migration was already underway. The wording at the time was direct: check the repository path before proceeding with daemon configuration; stop if the path does not exist, is not a directory, or the check cannot establish that the repository can continue to be used. The intent was also to add release information to the error object at the same point, so the failure text users saw would not depend on a particular caller.

There were two candidate locations for this work.

The first option was to keep both validation and error reporting near configuration migration. The advantage was a single gate covering the stages before and after migration; at the time, this was also thought to reduce the opportunities for callers to assess repository state themselves. The trade-off was that error report content would be tied to the migration flow: a change that should only add diagnostic information might change where errors were presented because of a repository-validation branch.

The second option was to keep only repository rejection close to the actual check, leaving platform release information to error construction or a reporting path further upstream. Each change would then have a narrow scope, but review would need to confirm whether validation failures could retain their original error identity, and whether the reporting path actually had access to platform release information. The initial draft did not choose the second option, mainly because the user paths for these two issues had not been separated out at the time.

The old starting point for reading the code was `src/move-repository-location.js`. The issue title and call name pointed there at the time, making it a suitable starting point for examining the path, existence checks, and directory checks; that is not a basis for treating this file as the owner of all daemon validation. The early notes implicitly made that attribution, though. This passage was left in during later review because some old links still start here.

The expectations for the first option were overstated as well: rejection before migration seemed sufficient to guarantee that there would be no additional visible changes. That expectation was not supported by an actual reproduction. The failure of the old call with an invalid repository was later logged as IPD-207. The card requires reproducing it from the pre-call state and checking whether any additional visible changes remain after completion. The focus here is not just "whether an error is reported," but what has already happened before the failure, and whether the UI or configuration has already been touched by the time the failure returns.

The repository path should not be used as evidence for the platform release information work, either. The record for IPD-224 limits that work to triggering "Include platform release in error reports" with existing tests or examples, then recording any uncovered user paths on the card. In other words, the established direction is to check whether error reports can include the required information, not to assume that every repository rejection naturally goes through the same reporting exit point.

After review, the original shared entry point is no longer the preferred option. The recommendation retained is to start with a small-scope experiment:

- Observe near the repository check whether rejection happens before migration actions, and record the visible state before and after failure.
- Use existing tests or examples to enter the error reporting path, and independently confirm whether platform release information appears.
- Discuss combining the two only if both paths actually share the same error construction point; sharing a call name is not enough.

This revision does not mean the two issues are unrelated. Both affect what information users can get when daemon startup fails, but they serve different purposes: the former determines which repositories will not be used further, while the latter determines what diagnostic context is also retained in the failure information. Observing them separately makes it possible to tell whether validation is in the wrong place or the report is missing information.

The conditions for dropping the assumptions changed accordingly. If the repository check cannot confirm that processing stops before migration, first drop the assumption that "the configuration entry point is early enough"; if the error reporting test path differs from the repository rejection path, drop the assumption that "one error object can cover both." Neither requires canceling the other piece of work as well; the requirement is only to avoid baking in an unverified shared boundary.

Three questions remain unanswered. First, whether a corrupt repository and a simply missing path reach the same decision point in existing calls. Second, whether "additional visible changes" after failure means configuration contents, the migration location, or merely error presentation. Third, whether missing platform release information in uncovered user paths is due to an omission at the reporting entry point or to tests not triggering the same branch. IPD-207 and IPD-224 remain the starting points for reproducing the first two types of issue and for checking report coverage, respectively; until results are available, do not turn these questions into conclusions.

One other boundary was not explored at the time: investigation of silent daemon failures should remain within the scope of DOC-17. This page addresses only repository rejection and error report information; it does not attribute the "no output" symptom to this trial proposal.

This page is therefore useful to retain as a record of the approaches considered during review: both the initial judgment to combine the work and the later judgment to split it are preserved, helping explain why the old call entry point drew attention. Before making actual changes, the validation and reporting points should still be determined by reproduction results for their respective paths.

# Application and Web UI Readiness Decision Record

When Kubo 0.13 was closed out, quality records often retained only one ready. This wording conflated the desktop application being usable with Web UI being ready, making it difficult later to determine which part of the startup flow had a problem.

The decision at the time was to retain two record points: application ready and Web UI ready. The application record only indicates that the desktop side reached a usable stage; the Web UI record only indicates that Web UI is ready. Recording only one final success was considered, but it cannot distinguish a desktop readiness failure from a Web UI readiness failure. Nor were separate records added for every startup detail; there were not enough samples at the closeout stage to support that level of granularity.

This time, the two records are not merged into "fully ready," nor is a fixed order prescribed. A user being able to enter Web UI does not by itself prove that the desktop record has been established; the reverse also applies. If older records treat the two as the same state, they need to be revisited using this distinction.

Trace back from `src/webui/index.js`. It is the Web UI reference point left by the earlier investigation; use it first to confirm the adjacent calls in the frozen revision. At that time, the emission point for the desktop-side record had not yet been finalized on this page.
