# Application and Web UI Readiness Decision Record

As the desktop work for Kubo 0.13 was being wrapped up, quality records often collapsed "the desktop is usable" and "Web UI is ready" into a single ready status. The two occur close together within the same startup, and issue descriptions often retain only one outcome, so the first version addressed what the records meant rather than rushing to add more names to the startup process.

## Initial choice

Keep two recording points: application readiness and Web UI readiness. The former answers whether the desktop has reached a usable state; the latter answers whether Web UI is ready. They can occur during the same startup, but that does not make them the same record. No requirement for them to occur in a fixed order was set at the time.

Recording only a single final success was rejected. That would not show whether a failure occurred before the desktop was ready or before Web UI was ready. Another option was to split every startup detail into a sequence of records; there were not enough call samples at the time to support that level of granularity, and adding names would only make the old quality records harder to compare. The decision therefore stopped at two distinguishable readiness states, without wrapping them in a single "fully ready" event.

The first draft also retained an old troubleshooting rule of thumb: if a user can access Web UI, the desktop application can be considered ready. This was not a confirmed equivalence. It reflected only the simplified framing used to investigate issues at the time and is retained here because older records carry it forward; when reviewing those records, this statement must not be used to infer the trigger conditions for the other record.

## Starting points retained for review

On the Web UI side, `src/webui/index.js` remains the starting point for investigation. This path can help confirm local adjacency relationships in the old revision, but it does not provide a complete account of the records in the desktop startup process. Changing the relationship between the two records requires both the actual invocation details and the user-visible result; it must not be based on guesses from the record names alone.

The goal of IPD-211 is to find the actual call behind the most recent report of "Record application and Web UI readiness metrics" and fill in how it was called and what the user saw. The card uses `Error` as its public search term. In its subsequent history, a support case was linked first, and it then moved from To Do to In Progress. These actions show that the retrospective investigation has a starting point, but they do not establish the order of the two records or a shared source for them in this document.

If the review only shows that Web UI is accessible, it supports at most the Web UI readiness side; if it only shows that the desktop window is still running, that does not automatically establish the Web UI side either. The two results should be attached to their respective records. Whether the application record and the Web UI record come from the same startup branch remains unresolved until a single piece of evidence shows both.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "Application ready" as ApplicationReady
    state "Web UI ready" as WebUIReady
    ApplicationReady: Desktop has reached a usable state
    WebUIReady: Web UI is ready
    note right of ApplicationReady
      Both records can occur during the same startup
      No order is specified
    end note
```

This page records the recording granularity considered at the time and the judgments made during the retrospective investigation; it is not a complete definition of the startup interface. Later material can correct the old statement, but the fact that the task has moved into active work does not justify stating the unconfirmed shared branch as fact. It is still cited in Quality and Regression material, so the initial single-value framing will not be deleted. # DHT routing adjustment proposal

As part of Desktop's closeout for Kubo 0.13, forced DHT client routing is a default behavior that should be confirmed separately. The current working assumption is that Desktop should no longer lock in this routing choice on the user's behalf; however, deleting the related configuration alone is not enough. The resulting configuration after startup and the return status received by the caller must remain identifiable.

The plan is to start at `src/daemon/config.js`, review what is written during configuration generation and migration, then trace actual references to check where the routing value is fixed. At this stage, do not treat the path as indicating implementation ownership; use it only as the location closest to the configuration change.

There are two options:

- Directly remove the client routing imposed by Desktop and record the post-upgrade configuration diff;
- Keep the status quo and move only the routing decision to the call site.

The first is the tentative choice because the second still leaves Desktop implicitly deciding Kubo's routing policy, making it difficult later to say who should change the default value.

During the trial, compare one existing configuration with one migrated configuration. If removal changes the parameter order, or if the caller cannot determine from the actual return status whether startup has completed, revert this adjustment and restore the original fixed behavior. The question of whether existing repositories retain the old value after migration remains unresolved.

# DHT Routing Change Proposal

This change was originally described as "removing a default." After review, it can no longer be described that way: if Desktop's configuration layer pins client routing for Kubo, an upgrade may leave old configuration in place and may also lead callers to mistake a configuration change for a startup result. The goal is for Desktop to stop making routing policy decisions without disturbing the argument order or actual return status visible in the existing CLI case.

`src/daemon/config.js` remains the starting point for this check. It sits near configuration assembly and migration, making it a useful place to first determine whether the routing value is set during new configuration generation, filled in for an existing configuration, or overridden before startup. Subsequent references must be based on the actual call relationships found; do not attribute all routing decisions to configuration migration just because a value appears near that file.

## State after review

IPD-212 documents a regression in post-upgrade results, not just a cleanup task. The item was later classified as a failure-type issue, showing that the initial draft's assumption that "simply removing the forced setting is enough" did not hold up in real-world use of the released version. The card description requires the current release to preserve argument order and actual return status when handling this CLI case; these two external constraints matter more than the internal configuration object.

Another review did not reach a complete conclusion. One known point remains unconfirmed and needs a rerun through the same entry point; the person continuing the checks also changed after the on-call schedule was adjusted. This means we cannot yet declare any single configuration difference the root cause, let alone claim verified compatibility for a branch that has not been rerun.

The draft's "remove it first, then look at callers" sequence needs to be corrected. The counterexample is that even if forced routing ultimately does need to be removed, callers do not necessarily depend on the routing value itself; they may depend on argument order or the status returned on failure. Deleting first and fixing things afterward would leave the regression samples without a comparable baseline.

## Proposed approach

This trial will change only the layer where Desktop imposes a routing choice, without copying Kubo's routing policy elsewhere. The checks should follow three steps in sequence:

1. Identify the places where configuration creation and configuration migration may each write forced DHT client routing, and record whether they share the same handling logic.
2. Observe routing field changes in existing configurations and post-migration configurations separately. If an existing value is simply a legacy remnant, handle it separately from the question of whether this change continues to force writes; cleaning up old values cannot substitute for removing the default behavior.
3. Follow the IPD-212 reference to the CLI entry point to check argument order and return status. Any conclusions here apply only to that entry point: success does not mean all startup paths have been covered, and failure does not automatically prove that the configuration layer is the only cause.

The recommendation is to treat "removal" as stopping Desktop from writing or overriding this client routing choice, rather than deleting a related string whenever it is found in any configuration. This preserves the distinction between users' existing configurations and this migration, and lets later differences be interpreted in terms of their source.

## Options compared at the time

**Stop forcing writes outright.** This is the recommended option for the trial. It puts routing policy back within the scope that Kubo and user configuration can express, leaving Desktop responsible only for its own configuration generation and migration. The trade-off is that old, migrated, and newly created configurations may take different forms and must be compared in the same CLI case.

**Keep forcing writes and only fix return handling.** This option can reduce the scope of short-term changes, but it does not address the issue that Desktop should no longer make routing choices after an upgrade. It can only serve as a fallback state and should not be presented as the final solution.

**Add a new compatibility switch.** Not adopting this at this stage. The available material does not show a need for an additional configuration surface; until the routing value's source and the regression branch have been determined, adding a switch would only add another layer to explain along the migration path.

## Rollback conditions

If any of the following occurs after rerunning through the same CLI entry point, this trial should be rolled back: argument order changes; the actual return status no longer distinguishes between the original success and failure cases; or migration overwrites a user's existing routing choice with a new default. On rollback, restore Desktop's previous pinning behavior and retain the configuration samples that caused the differences; do not just revert the code and close the issue.

The remaining unconfirmed points are whether all relevant values in old configurations came from previous Desktop writes, and whether the failure-type issue occurs only on the post-upgrade migration path. The former determines whether to start a separate cleanup effort; the latter determines the review scope for this change. This proposal should not present either as an established fact.

# PATH and npm startup troubleshooting tree

When you receive a regression report that says "the removed PATH or npm startup hooks are still in use," don't immediately attribute the `ipfs` text in the error to the Desktop startup flow. This runbook covers remnants of legacy startup entry points in the Kubo 0.13 cleanup, not configuration key cleanup or the controller's own availability.

## Start with enough detail to choose a branch

At a minimum, the report should include the raw startup output and the action that triggered it. If all you have is a UI message, the contents of PATH in a terminal, or a paraphrased report, collect those two items first; without startup context, stop the investigation here.

Start the investigation at `src/npm-on-ipfs/index.js`. Open the currently frozen version and record the function name, string, or call site involved in the report. Don't take npm in the path name as proof that the code there still starts npm.

## The report points to npm-on-ipfs

If you find only names, imports, or historical comments near this entry point, with no call that can reach a startup action, record it as a "navigation hit." Go back to the reporter for the actual call stack or startup output; don't close out the regression based on this hit.

If you can trace the call site in the report to a legacy npm startup action, capture the function name and the immediately adjacent output, and confirm that it happens during application startup rather than in a manually run standalone script. Once confirmed, check whether that same action is still triggered by old configuration or environment inputs; record these two cases separately in the issue, rather than lumping them together as "npm wasn't fully removed."

## The report only involves PATH

If the output is just the shell's PATH, with no call site in the Desktop startup chain, stop at the environment layer first. The fact that PATH still contains a particular directory doesn't mean the application will look there for the daemon.

If the startup output clearly shows that path lookup was involved in starting the daemon, record whether the lookup happened beforehand or after the failure. In the former case, continue tracing the startup entry point; in the latter, save the failure output first to avoid mistaking later diagnostic output for the cause.

## When the investigation can end

If you can confirm that the report concerns a manually run script or displayed environment information, or that no application startup action was reached, record the basis for that determination and end this investigation. If you can confirm that the legacy entry point is still being called, don't change the compatibility policy here; attach a minimal reproduction and the call site, and route it back to the corresponding cleanup task.

# Feature Configuration Key Migration Guide

This record began with a narrow focus: a Kubo 0.13 desktop convergence check drew attention to feature configuration keys, rather than to a clearly named configuration module. The initial draft followed `src/tray.js` and, after seeing configuration, storage, and two feature declarations, sketched out a migration direction. The wording at the time was "centralize the keys and have callers use the same entry point". That sentence is retained here because it really was the working assessment at the time; it is not proof of a completed migration.

The sketch left at the time is shown below, with arrows indicating the investigation order, not a call graph verified against the source code:

```text
Old path: Feature flag read sites ──> Scattered key names ──> Old settings in the store
New path: Centralized key location ──> Feature callers ──> Compatibility migration for the store
```

Tracing the old path began with terms inside the file. These direct bindings can in fact be seen in `src/tray.js`:

```text
const i18n = require('i18next')
const path = require('path')
const addToIpfs = require('./add-to-ipfs')
const logger = require('./common/logger')
```

The same location also identifies `store`, `moveRepositoryLocation`, and `runGarbageCollector`. The early investigation therefore included configuration, settings, automatic, garbage, automaticgc, setting, auto, and launch in its search scope. This list is useful for reproducing how files were found at the time, but it does not mean that all these terms represent fields whose migration has been completed. `i18n` and `path` are dependencies adjacent to the file; they do not by themselves establish ownership of the feature keys.

### Migration Order Used in the Initial Draft

First record the actual name and storage location of the old setting, then find the feature that reads it directly. Only in the second step should you compare the naming of the centralized keys, to avoid changing strings first and discovering later that another entry point still consumes the old setting. For the two categories of terms, automatic garbage collection and launch, the initial draft only called for checking them separately, not combining them into a single flag. Handle compatibility values only at the end: first make sure existing settings can be read, then let the new centralized entry point take over writes.

This sequence is an operational recommendation in the record, and cannot be used to infer that a complete migration batch already exists. The document records neither a batch number nor a change list for any caller. The so-called "compatible callers" still need to be investigated here, and the location of `src/tray.js` cannot substitute for call relationships.

### How Rollback Was Described

The early version described only one recovery approach: if startup or feature flag reads behave abnormally after migration, temporarily restore the old key read path, disable the new centralized entry point, and observe the results using the original settings. Here, "restoring the old path" has no corresponding command, diff, or specific filename; it describes an action that was planned at the time, not a record of a rollback that has already been run. Do not treat this paragraph as the current release procedure.

### Corrections Retained After Review

The later review added locations within the file, but did not fill in the missing call chain. `src/tray.js:2` is the `i18n` binding, `:3` is `path`, `:4` is `addToIpfs`, and `:5` is `logger`; `store` is at `:6`, `moveRepositoryLocation` is at `:7`, and `runGarbageCollector` is at `:8`. These points are enough to explain why the earlier investigation led to this file, and provide a starting point for tracing back from here. They are not enough to establish where the centralized keys are defined, all the readers, or the layer where migration writes take place.

So the initial draft's claim that "this file is responsible for configuration migration" must now be narrowed to "this file contains the configuration-related connections visible in the earlier investigation". # Main Process Event Channel Decision Record

In the wrap-up of Kubo 0.13, main-process event channels can't remain scattered across individual feature actions. The tentative direction is to put the channel names and entry points in one location for later lookup; tray will still retain the combination of menu, status, and actions, and the entire `src/tray.js` will not be treated as the place where channels are defined.

We initially started by looking at tray because this file brings in `i18next`, `path`, `./add-to-ipfs`, and `./common/logger`, and also touches store, repository location migration, and garbage collection. These objects can all appear near a UI action, but that doesn't mean their event conventions are all owned by tray. The file looks more like an entry point for observing where main-process actions converge.

We compared two approaches at the time. One was to keep a copy of the channel names near each action module, with a smaller change set; the other was to first consolidate the names and listener conventions, then have existing actions plug in according to their original responsibilities. The latter is tentatively adopted. During review, first determine whether an event is part of a convention between main processes, then determine whether tray initiates it, consumes it, or only presents the result.

Still not fully mapped: which actions in existing user flows go through a unified entry point; whether configuration migration has exceptions that need separate handling.

versions.body:
# Main Process Event Channel Decision Record

The starting point for this consolidation was not to turn tray into the main process's overall controller. The earlier investigation drew attention to `src/tray.js`: this file places UI text, paths, add-content actions, logs, configuration access, repository-location migration, and garbage collection side by side as adjacent objects. This kind of adjacency easily leads people to treat "actions initiated from tray" and "event channels defined by tray" as the same thing. The conclusion retained after review is that the two must not be conflated.

The initial draft only recorded the direction and did not make the trade-offs and scope clear. This record keeps the decision focused on the main-process events themselves, rather than grouping all code that passes through tray into the same change. This centralization is also not about replacing one large file with another; it requires names, declaration locations, and listener conventions to have stable maintenance points, so reviewers can start checking event relationships from one place.

## Decision

The names, declaration locations, and listener conventions for main-process event channels will be maintained centrally. Each feature module will continue to retain its own action implementation; when it needs to initiate or subscribe to a main-process event, it will connect according to the unified convention.

This decision covers the organization of the channels, not a reassignment of ownership for functional actions. tray is responsible for organizing user-visible state and operations; action modules are responsible for their respective business behavior; the centralized maintenance point is responsible for giving cross-module events reviewable names and an entry point. The three layers may meet in a single user operation, but they should not be merged into the same layer of responsibility merely because they meet.

The initial draft's conclusion to "first lock down the channel entry point, then have existing actions connect" remains valid. The added limitation is that connecting does not mean moving the action implementation, nor does it mean requiring all main-process logic to go through tray. An action can remain in its original module and simply emit or receive events according to the unified convention while still complying with this decision.

## Clues from tray

`src/tray.js` is the UI convergence point for this follow-up review. The opening declarations that can be located directly are as follows:

```js
const i18n = require('i18next')
const path = require('path')
const addToIpfs = require('./add-to-ipfs')
const logger = require('./common/logger')
```

These declarations show that tray needs to handle localized text, paths, add-content actions, and local logs. The file also contains bindings for `store`, `moveRepositoryLocation`, and `runGarbageCollector`. They show that this location touches configuration and maintenance operations, and also that the objects around the menu code are not all of one kind.

Therefore, the import relationships in the file cannot directly answer "who defines this event". For example, `i18n` and `path` support tray's localized-text or resource-location handling; `logger` is primarily adjacent to local records; `addToIpfs`, moving the repository location, and garbage collection represent different action entry points. A menu item may call an action module, but there is no reason for it to thereby become the authoritative location for all event names of that action.

The earlier investigation's path from issue names and call names to this file was a valuable starting point: it helps people find where a user-visible operation may connect with main-process behavior. But this clue by itself does not establish implementation ownership. During review, the judgment should continue to be based on the actual channel declarations and call relationships, rather than substituting menu structure for event relationships.

## Options considered

### Naming each action in place

The first approach is to keep naming distributed: whichever main-process action needs to send a notification writes its own channel name nearby in its module. Its advantage is that local changes are short, and reading a particular action does not require leaving the current file. For a single local callback that will not be subscribed to by other modules, this style also does not immediately create a visible problem.

The reason it was not adopted is not that any existing name is necessarily wrong, but that review cost turns into memory cost as the number of actions grows. Reviewers cannot confirm from one place whether an event with the same name already exists, and it is difficult to confirm that listeners are still handling it according to the same convention. A constant change may update only the initiating point or only one listener point; after seeing an action in the menu code, it is even harder to tell whether another location uses a different name to express a similar state.

The Kubo 0.13 consolidation needs event relationships that can be traced back. Distributed naming preserves the convenience of each local change, but continues to make readers stitch together the name mapping file by file, so it is not the direction for this round.

### Put all handling in tray

The second approach is to centralize all channel handling in tray. It initially appears direct: tray already touches multiple user actions, so putting notifications and listeners there seems sufficient to provide an entry point.

It was not adopted. tray's responsibilities include menu organization, state presentation, text and resource handling, and invoking business actions. Pulling all event conventions into this file would bind UI organization to cross-module names. `addToIpfs`, `moveRepositoryLocation`, and `runGarbageCollector`, which represent actions of different kinds, would be forced to share a UI-layer entry point simply because they are all around the menu. The result would be a larger tray module, not a clearer channel boundary.

This style would also create a misleading review implication: as if main-process events that do not pass through the menu were outside the unified convention, or as if any event initiated from the menu must have its name stored by tray. Both implications run counter to the goal of this decision.

### Centralize the channel layer as a separate concern

The third approach, and the final decision, is to centralize the channel layer as a separate concern, without causing the call sites for actions to lose their original responsibilities. Menu text, path computation, log recording, and action implementations do not need to be rewritten for channel centralization. If a tray action needs to trigger or subscribe to a main-process event, it should connect to the unified convention; it can still retain its own menu semantics and action implementation.

This choice allows incremental integration by call site. It does not promise to cover all user paths at once, nor does it claim that every existing action has completed migration. What the decision fixes first is the verification method: for a cross-module event, first check the name and listener convention from the unified maintenance point; for a purely local UI action, there is no need to force in a channel layer for formal consistency.

## Boundary for review

To determine whether an object belongs to this centralization, first check whether it expresses an event convention that needs to be shared between main processes. If so, the name and listener rules should be traced back from the unified entry point. If it only helps tray handle text, icons, menus, or a particular action invocation, it should still be read according to its local responsibility and should not be moved into the channel layer merely because it is near event-related code.

This allows the following cases to be handled separately:

- When a menu item invokes an action such as `addToIpfs`, the menu trigger and the action implementation remain two separate places to inspect; whether a cross-module event exists depends on the actual channel relationship.
- `store` appears in the area adjacent to tray, indicating that the UI may read or change configuration; this is not enough to classify configuration keys or configuration migration as a channel declaration.
- `moveRepositoryLocation` and `runGarbageCollector` show that tray can reach maintenance operations; they do not automatically prove that tray should hold the event names for those operations.
- Changes that only modify translations, paths, or logs should not be counted as part of channel centralization unless the changes also alter an event convention that is already centrally maintained.

This is not about establishing a separate test for every action, but about avoiding the mistake of treating "where the user clicks in" as "where the event is defined". The object of this round's check is whether the name and entry point are consistent, not requiring all actions to be close in the file layout or requiring every main-process action to go through tray.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> TrayAction
    TrayAction --> LocalAction: Local menu or state operation
    TrayAction --> ChannelReview: Requires main-process event convention
    ChannelReview --> CentralizedChannel: Check name and listener convention
    LocalAction --> [*]
    CentralizedChannel --> [*]
```

`TrayAction` in the diagram is only the starting point for a user-visible action; it does not mean that tray owns all subsequent implementation. `ChannelReview` is the review fork: only cases that need a cross-module event convention enter the centralized maintenance point. Local handling stops at the local action layer; no extra channel is created merely to satisfy a uniform form.

## Associations that need correction in the initial draft

The initial draft placed the main-process event channel and configuration migration too close together, making it easy to read them as two things that one refactoring could explain simultaneously. This wording is now corrected: configuration migration has its own compatibility issues; the presence of `store` in tray, or adjacency to repository-location migration, is not grounds for concluding that it must change along with channel centralization.

Bundled Kubo compatibility also cannot be inferred from this decision. A correction remained from the subsequent review: the Configuration migration and bundled Kubo compatibility section still has one unconfirmed point. This unconfirmed item is retained here to prevent a conjecture that they may share part of an implementation from being written as an established association. Channel centralization only addresses how names and listener conventions are maintained; it neither authorizes changes to configuration migration semantics nor concludes the bundled Kubo compatibility assessment.

This is also why `src/tray.js` was not designated as the sole change-entry point. That path is suitable for finding locations where UI actions and the main process may meet, but configuration migration, Kubo compatibility, and the event channel remain different review objects. If it is later confirmed that they share an implementation location, that relationship should be recorded separately rather than combining the three issues into one change package.

## Relationship to IPD-216

IPD-216 retains the observation that support for existing user paths is part of this consolidation, and requires that, after triggering the path with existing tests or examples, any paths not yet covered be written back to the card. The card is suitable for carrying the question "Which user path is not covered?", but it does not replace the decision here about how channels are organized.

The card was later moved to a different implementation section as a scope correction. This indicates that the clues initially seen from tray are not the same as the final implementation location; however, it does not overturn the centralization direction. The decision not to depend on tray as the sole entry point is precisely intended to ensure that, when the implementation location changes, the channel names and listener conventions still have a stable way to be traced back.

During follow-up review, confirmed local facts should be distinguished from facts that still need to be confirmed through call relationships. The former include the objects imported by the tray file and the action names appearing in it; the latter include whether a particular user path has connected to the unified entry point and whether any listeners are missing. The menu structure can help locate the first category of clues, but it cannot replace checking the second category.

## Items outside this round

User paths that are not yet covered should be written back to IPD-216, rather than starting another set of channel names beside the tray file. This way, the card records coverage gaps and the centralized maintenance point records the event convention; neither will encroach on the other's responsibilities.

The unconfirmed relationship between configuration migration and bundled Kubo compatibility will be decided separately once the corresponding implementation location is available. There is currently not enough material to explain it as a side effect of channel centralization, and they should not be bound together merely because both were raised during the consolidation phase.

This decision ends here: main-process event channels will be maintained centrally, and tray will remain the composition point for UI and actions. Later reviews should check whether the names, declaration locations, and listener conventions are consistent; they should not expand a single import, menu action, or card adjustment into a broader attribution of implementation ownership. When a requirement changes a channel name or another observable behavior that an existing repository test checks, that test may be renamed or adjusted so it still checks the behavior. The create-toggler checks may listen for configUpdated and toggle_${option} through the shared IPC event names instead of the previous string literals. The launch checks may add the existing-repository connection-manager case: GracePeriod 300s, LowWater 50, and HighWater 300 migrate to GracePeriod 1m, LowWater 20, and HighWater 40. Do not delete, skip, or weaken an assertion that the requirement does not change. Production source and required dependency metadata remain the other allowed edits.

title: Private Repository Blocking Proposal

versions.body:
# Private Repository Blocking Proposal

As the Kubo 0.13 work was wrapping up, private-network repositories came up in the daemon configuration discussion. This is not a repository repair record. It captures the blocking approach we were preparing to try at the time: once the configuration flow detects this type of repository, stop treating it as a normal state in which startup can proceed. For the entry point, start with `src/daemon/config.js`; reviewers considered it sufficient to support this check and the subsequent message.

## Scope of the proposed trial

The block applies only to private-network repositories, not to general daemon configuration problems. Users need to know that startup did not continue because of the repository type, rather than having that message folded into a generic startup failure. The configuration layer owns this branch; repository migration and connection policy stay in their respective handling paths. Otherwise, a single safeguard would also cut off unrelated recovery paths.

There was a more aggressive suggestion at the time: if the repository is rejected during configuration, downstream controllers no longer need to concern themselves with it. That suggestion was not adopted as a decision. It assumed that all entry points went through the same configuration check, but the callers still in use had not been checked. It also did not specify which diagnostic information should be retained after an existing repository was identified. This paragraph is kept here so later investigations do not mistake "blocking" for completed end-to-end isolation.

## Trade-offs

The smaller option was to stop immediately in the configuration branch when a private-network repository was detected and show a dedicated message. This would keep the check close to repository configuration; the trade-off was that callers relying on the standard error format from later in startup might get a different result.

Another option was for the configuration layer to only flag the state and let the startup flow handle rejection centrally. This would consolidate error reporting, but would move the repository-type rejection further from the check. It would also require confirming that ordinary configuration updates would not overwrite the state. The review leaned toward trying the former first, because the goal of this change was to block these repositories, not to reorganize the daemon lifecycle.

## Withdrawal criteria and open checks

If existing callers show that rejecting during configuration would obscure the original diagnostics, or if private-network repositories cannot be distinguished from invalid repositories in general, drop this placement and instead retain only the detection result before deciding on the entry point. We still need to find an actual caller and check the version it uses, where it enters configuration, and its current behavior. Until then, this proposal should not be treated as a compatibility commitment already in place. During verification, also retain the original diagnostics, the point of rejection, and the actual entry point.

# Quality Signal Desk Window-End Checklist

**Trigger**: Before the window ends, use only the current entry point to handle borrowing, final output, return timing, and the withdrawal entry point for adj-dialogs. ## Before the window ends

1. [ ] After finding `connection manager`, confirm that this borrowing still corresponds to the current window, and leave the final output in its original location. If you can't find the entry point, stop; don't continue searching based on similar names.

2. [ ] Don't clean up the environment when you see `IPC channel`. First preserve the output in place, then check whether `error identity` has appeared. The old rule requires stopping here if `error identity` hasn't appeared; continue to apply this check according to the checklist from that time, rather than switching to a different check at window end.

3. [ ] Once the final output has been left in place, check the return timing. The return must not happen before the output; if the output is not yet complete, maintain the borrowed state and stop the subsequent return and withdrawal actions.

4. [ ] When returning, use only adj-dialogs's registered withdrawal entry point. Don't clean up through other entry points next to `connection manager`, and don't withdraw unconfirmed objects along with it. If the withdrawal entry point can't be found, preserve the original state and stop.

5. [ ] After completing the return, review whether any unhandled output or incorrect identities remain within the window. If you find anything missed, go back to the "preserve the final output" step; don't go on to declare the window closed.

## Stop conditions

If any of the following occurs, stop the checklist here: the current entry point can't be confirmed, the final output hasn't been retained, `error identity` hasn't appeared, the return timing is unclear, or the withdrawal entry point for adj-dialogs is unavailable. Stop cleanup and preserve the borrowed state and existing output; don't substitute an alternate-path name for the entry point.

# Quality Signal Console Cache Trade-off Record

This records a trade-off made at the time of dialogs-quality-signal, not a plan to redesign the Quality Signal Console. What was available during the handoff window was the current revision; returning to the original setup would require rebuilding the environment. The two options differed in time cost and in the kind of failure sample they would yield.

The choice at the time was to preserve the current revision as a starting point for later review, without rebuilding the environment for this inventory. That choice prioritized repeatable review of existing material, rather than asserting that the cache could replace the original setup. The original setup may still have included runtime conditions that were not preserved; there simply wasn't enough reason in that round to start a separate rebuild for it.

Another way to split the material was discussed: continue collecting along `BrowserWindow`, or pull `analytics event` out on its own. The reason for favoring the latter was narrow: the two failure exits seen in `docs/adj-dialogs/decisions/dialogs-quality-signal-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoff.md` were different. Listing the event separately would at least avoid lumping the two exits into a single window issue at the outset.

The objection was that retaining the revision could easily lead people to mistake a later successful sample for an explanation of the same batch. The record therefore still needs to locate the current entry point for the first failure; successful samples are kept only for comparison. "Being able to see the cache" was not treated as the canary having passed, nor was it used to draw a conclusion about release diagnostics.

The decision centered on the migration revision: the existing material would first be handed over with the revision, and the rollback entry point would also be retained in its known state. Whether a rollback should restore only the old entry point was not decided at the time; which callers were then using release diagnostics had not been established either. The cache contents cannot answer either question.

The costs of the rejected approach were added during the meeting, and the results of the exit action were retained as supplementary material. They did not change the context of the original choice: the priority in this round was to preserve an inspectable revision, then decide whether rebuilding the environment was worth the cost. One review changed only the wording, not the facts observed at the time.

This record may still be cited, but it should be read within the time frame of that trade-off. # Troubleshooting Tree for a Stuck Quality Signal Console

This page addresses a very narrow situation: the current entry point shows dialogs-quality-signal stuck, but it is not yet clear whether to keep investigating the Quality Signal Console, check the exit action, or hand the issue to the permissions owner. Preserve what you see first, then follow the tree. The tree stops at the first point where new evidence is needed; do not substitute a results summary for missing records.

## Save the Entry-Point State First

At the start, preserve the current entry point's text or state exactly as it appears, and note when you first saw it. Separately save the version in use, the current revision, and the value left at the current entry point when the window ends. Here, specify whether the "entry point" is the standard entry point or the entry point containing the internal results; do not record both as a single "page state". Copy the original text rather than paraphrasing whenever possible; in particular, do not distinguish between an empty value, an old value, and nothing being displayed.

An early draft only asked people to first find `IPC channel`, then record `error identity`, and finally stop if there was no `repository validation`. These three observations are still useful, but they are not automatic classifiers. You must first be able to find the entry-point records before deciding on the next branch. If there are no raw records, collect them first; do not infer that the Quality Signal Console has failed from an error name that has already been cleaned up.

Previously, someone reran first and only went back to look for the failure sample after getting a green result. The environment differences from before the retry were not preserved, so it was later impossible to determine whether the green result still corresponded to the original entry point. The order is now fixed: save the first failure sample, save the version and environment from that time, and only then perform any reruns. A rerun result can be a new observation, but it must not overwrite the first failure result.

## Branch Based on Symptoms

```text
The current entry point shows dialogs-quality-signal stuck
├─ No corresponding raw records
│  └─ Collect missing evidence: preserve the text, time, version, and end-of-window value, then stop
└─ Raw records are available
   ├─ No comparable normal daemon startup sample yet
   │  └─ Record only the isolated observation; do not attribute a cause
   └─ A normal sample is available
      ├─ The first difference is in the current entry point, an old cache, or an old task
      │  └─ Check the entry-point records; stop if no cache or task evidence can be found
      └─ The first difference is in the dialogs-quality-signal records
         ├─ Has not yet reached repository validation
         │  └─ Stay within this project and collect the missing validation inputs
         └─ Has reached repository validation
            ├─ Still involves the project's own resources, permissions, or indexes
            │  └─ Route to the in-project maintenance entry point
            └─ Requires changing user-visible behavior or crossing an explicit interface
               └─ Stop this tree and hand off to the permissions owner or open a separate review
```

"Raw records are available" does not mean having a single line with a final conclusion. At a minimum, you must be able to see the inputs before and after the failure and place them alongside the most recent normal `daemon startup` sample from the same entry point. If you only have a failure sample and no normal sample, you can only state what appeared at the entry point on that occasion, not how it differed from a normal startup.

Change only one condition when comparing. You can hold dialogs-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command constant, replacing only the current revision; you can also hold the revision constant and then change the environment, but you must not change the command, entry point, and revision at the same time. If two conditions change together, return to the collection branch, because the next difference you see cannot be clearly attributed. This branch does not require finding the ultimate cause first; it only requires preserving the first visible difference.

## Making Decisions When Records Are Available

First, arrange the normal and failure samples for `daemon startup` chronologically and find the first difference. Do not infer the intermediate process from averages, directory names, or the display on the final page. If the first difference is that the current entry point still shows an old value, preserve the window's end time, then check for an old cache or an old task. If there are no cache records, task records, or other materials connecting these two points in time, stop at the old entry-point value; do not directly label it a failure of dialogs-quality-signal.

The situation preserved in IPDA-024 is that the current entry point still had the old value after the window ended. It serves as a reminder to preserve the end time, but is not enough on its own to establish whether the old value came from an old cache or an old task. If neither possibility has supporting records, write "The old value remained at the end of the window; source unconfirmed" in the handoff, rather than replacing the question mark with a component name.

If the first difference really does appear in dialogs-quality-signal's own records, first check whether the existing inputs are sufficient to reach `repository validation`. If it has not been reached, stay within the project and complete this step; once it has been reached, check whether the issue is still limited to this project's own resources, permissions, or indexes. If only these objects are affected, finish through the in-project maintenance entry point. If the next step requires changing the user-visible contract or crossing an explicit interface, stop the current tree rather than making an ad hoc behavioral decision in the runbook.

`repository validation` is a stopping point, not a root-cause label. It means troubleshooting has reached a point where another piece of evidence or a different boundary is needed. Even after it appears, the issue may still be internal to the project; it may also already require the permissions owner or a formal review. Routing depends on what must be accessed or changed next, not on whether the term itself looks like success or failure.

## Do Not Merge the Two Entry Points

IPDA-021 first recorded dialogs · Quality Signal Board and the exit action from before the environment switch. A later card record showed another contrast: the current result was present in the internal results, but absent from the standard entry point corresponding to the exit entry point. These observations must be recorded separately. The presence of internal results does not mean the standard entry point has recovered; a value at the standard entry point does not mean the Quality Signal Console's raw records are complete either.

The tree therefore treats the exit action as a separate observation. When confirming that the exit action occurred, record the entry point and time at which it happened; when confirming that the quality signal appeared, record its own raw records. If you can see only one of the two, stop at the missing one. Do not change "The current result is present in the internal results" to "All entry points have recovered", and do not rewrite the absence of a result at the standard entry point as daemon startup having failed.

The adjacent records in IPDA-023 show that the rollback states of dialogs-quality-s and the exit action were inconsistent; the card also retained the note "The expiration action is present, but the execution record from that run before the failure was not saved". When you encounter the same pattern, check the rollback entry point and the exit action separately, and first look for the execution record from before the failure. If you can only confirm that the expiration action exists, but have no pre-failure record, preserve only those two facts; the rollback state cannot stand in for that record.

Partial recovery must also be recorded separately. If one entry point has rolled back while another still shows the old state, record this as inconsistent states; do not write that the entire process is complete. Conversely, a result appearing in dialogs-quality-signal does not automatically prove that the exit entry point displayed the same result. Whichever item is missing should be listed as the next evidence needed, rather than continuing toward the end of the tree.

## revision Rerun Branch

The action in IPDA-022 holds dialogs-quality-signal, the current entry point, and the command constant, replacing only the current revision. This is a way to check whether the revision caused the first difference, not a way to restore the original state. If the execution record from before the failure was not saved before the rerun, return to the collection branch first; even if a new result appears again, do not fill in details that were absent from the original evidence.

When rerunning, list the changed condition separately and preserve the entry-point state after the rerun. If the result changes, write "The result changed after replacing the revision", then return to the two samples to find the first difference; do not directly state that the revision has been proven to be the cause. If the result does not change, that only means no change was observed with the entry point, command, and environment held constant in this run. If the command or environment also changes, the comparison is invalid and the evidence must be collected again.

The materials from before and after the environment switch come from different observation times. The records in IPDA-021 cannot be stitched together with rerun results into one continuous experiment; first label which materials are from before the switch and which are from after it, then determine whether they can be compared. If only the internal results remain, with no corresponding records from the standard entry point, stop along the missing-entry-point branch.

## Handoff and Stopping

For the handoff, include the first failure sample, the most recent normal daemon startup sample, the only condition that was changed, the node reached so far, and which records are still missing. You can write "repository validation has been observed; permissions have not yet been confirmed", or "The old value remained at the end of the window; no cache or task records were found". Do not rewrite "Permissions pending investigation" as an established permissions issue, and do not rewrite "The exit action was executed" as the user-visible state having recovered.

Keep the handoff entry point as `docs/adj-dialogs/runbooks/dialogs-quality-signal-stuck-escalation-contact.md`. It is the maintenance entry point for dialogs · Quality Signal Board, and the attachments are still maintained by adj-dialogs. IPDA-021, IPDA-022, IPDA-023, and IPDA-024 can be consulted for the environment switch, single-variable revision change, rollback inconsistency, and old value at the end of the window, respectively; they supplement the evidence from the situation, but do not replace the current node in this tree.

If the person on duty only has a compiled summary, look for the raw inputs first. Stop if they cannot be found; do not continue making inferences from the summary. If you only have permissions and no dialogs-quality-signal failure sample, take the collection branch; if you only have a failure sample and no normal daemon startup sample, record only the isolated observation. The tree does not skip over missing evidence, nor does it jump outside the project just because a rerun turns green.

If the next collection yields a recovery action, a permissions boundary, or an execution record from before the failure, append the new material after the corresponding branch. Without new evidence, keep the current stopping point.

When you see a stall at the current entry point, first check whether you have the original record. Here, "original record" means the input, version, request/run id, and first visible output captured on the first failure. It does not include green results from later reruns.

```text
Current entry point stalls
├─ No sample from the first failure
│  └─ Collect missing data only; don't change config first or discuss root cause
└─ Sample from the first failure available
```

## Preserve the evidence first

First, keep the original input, version, first visible result, and failure time for the current entry point on the original card. IPDB-017 later called for finding the first result on the current revision after the change; later green results must not overwrite that result. Reruns can help with comparisons, but do not establish recovery from the original failure.

If there is no record, collecting missing data is the only action. Do not infer intermediate behavior from directory names, averages, or the final displayed state. If a record is available, compare `daemon startup` against the most recent healthy sample and stop at the first difference; change only one condition at a time.

## Which branch to follow

If it fails at `repository validation`, first preserve the validation input and output. If the user-visible contract needs to change here later, stop using this page and move to formal review; this page is not a substitute for a design decision. # Release Automation Troubleshooting Tree

When the current entry point shows that the queue has stalled, but there is no new success or failure output, do not classify it as a build failure yet. First ask a narrow question: is the first failure sample still available? The tree below proceeds only as far as the evidence supports.

```text
Current entry point appears stuck
├─ No first failure sample
│  ├─ A later rerun has a green result: keep the green result, remain at evidence collection
│  └─ Not even a green result: add the current entry point output, version, and request/run id
└─ First failure sample is available
   ├─ The first output is a permission denial
   │  ├─ Denial occurs within pkgs-release-automation: check project permissions and resources
   │  └─ Denial occurs at a clearly defined interface: save the interface fields, hand off to the shared owner
   ├─ The first output stops at repository validation
   │  ├─ Only validating an index within the project: keep it within this project
   │  └─ Requires changing a user-visible contract: stop, send for formal review
   └─ Neither of the above
      ├─ Can be aligned with normal daemon startup: find the first environment difference
      └─ Cannot be aligned: leave it unknown, do not choose an owner based on the error name
```

The "first failure sample" is not the final page after a rerun. At a minimum, it must show the input at the time, the version, the first output, and the request/run id; if these items are scattered across screenshots and old links, preserve the originals first, then write a readable summary. A green rerun is useful, but it only shows that the run passed under those conditions and cannot erase the first failure.

## First Confirm What Happened at the Entry Point

Open `docs/adj-pkgs/runbooks/pkgs-release-automation-stuck-escalation-contact.md` and look for `error identity` first. The field names here may appear in the entry point output, or only in attachment names; neither location alone establishes a root cause. If there is only a vague error phrase, record the stage where it appeared, and do not fill in the object based on a directory name.

When the first sample is available, use the most recent normal `daemon startup` result as a baseline. Change only one condition for the comparison: use the same version in a different environment, or a different version in the same environment, and do not change the input, permissions, and entry point at the same time. Start by recording the first difference. If the difference is still within the build queue, artifact version, or index of pkgs-release-automation, continue investigating within the project; if the difference has already crossed a clearly defined interface, stop at that interface.

When the first sample is missing, the troubleshooting action is to collect the missing evidence. Do not start by clearing the queue, deleting attachments, rebuilding artifacts, or repeatedly clicking retry. Without the original input, a later "recovery" cannot be compared with the original incident. If only screenshots remain, preserve the time, version, and visible output in them; mark fields that are not visible as unknown, and do not fill them in from memory.

## The Permission Denial Branch

IPDB-015 recorded one failure to access a standard entry point. When trying adj-pkgs as a non-administrator, retain the denial location together with the request/run id; the four Chinese characters meaning "access failed" alone are not enough to determine whether the problem is with project permissions, a shared interface, or the entry point itself.

If the denial occurs in resources or indexes belonging to pkgs-release-automation itself, keep it within this project and have the on-duty maintainer check the permission configuration and queue objects. You can confirm whether the resources exist and whether the entry point still points to the same object, but do not describe upstream fields you have not yet seen as confirmed.

If the denial occurs at a clearly defined interface, stop investigating further downstream. First put the interface name, input fields, and first denial output on the original card, then hand off to the shared owner. IPDB-016 was once blocked because the owner of the core module's upstream interface had not confirmed the input fields; this status means that the fields remain unconfirmed, not that any project has taken ownership of the fix.

## The `repository validation` Branch

When you see `repository validation`, first save the input from before validation and the validation output. Do not treat artifacts regenerated after cleanup as the original artifacts, and do not overwrite the first result after the change with a later revision that passed. The action in IPDB-017 is to find the first current revision after the change; keep this record separate from subsequent green results.

If the validation failure only involves resources, permissions, or indexes within the project, continue investigating the corresponding objects. You can confirm whether the version identifiers, queue records, and artifacts all refer to the same item; you cannot infer that objects are the same version just because they share a name. IPDB-018 noted missing version identifiers for same-named pkgs-release-automation objects, so pin the toolchain first, then determine whether they are the same object.

If the fix requires changing a user-visible contract, troubleshooting stops here. Do not make a decision on behalf of the design review in the runbook, and do not describe one passing sample as a compatibility commitment. When handing off, include only the validation input, output, version, and branches already traversed; if these materials are unavailable, mark the missing items.

## Hot Caches and Premature Recovery

One old branch once treated the exit action as the endpoint of the current entry point. A later check found that the troubleshooting branch's expiration action came from a hot cache. A cache hit makes the page look complete, but that does not mean the current queue has actually completed. First note the cache conditions, then find the original output under the same conditions.

Another premature retry cleared the failure sample. After the retry went green, the original record contained only "success", leaving no way to answer whether the failure occurred during validation, in permissions, or at the entry point. If the same situation occurs now, stop recovery actions and first save the original input, version, and undo action. Resume comparison only after the samples from IPDB-014 are attached; without samples, remain at evidence collection and do not proceed into root-cause branches.

Do not directly treat `IPC channel`, `migration revision`, `tray lifecycle`, or `native theme`, terms from adjacent discussions, as failure stages of pkgs-release-automation. They may be search clues, but this page makes judgments only from the current entry point output and this project's build queue. Similar error names cannot substitute for the first difference either.

## When to Hand Off, and to Whom

| Object observed | Keep within this project or hand off | What to retain before handoff |
|---|---|---|
| Build queue, artifact version, index within the project | Keep within pkgs-release-automation | First output, version, queue object |
| Permission denial for project resources or a standard entry point | Keep within the project initially | Identity, denial location, request/run id |
| Denial or field mismatch beyond a clearly defined interface | Hand off to the shared owner | Interface fields, original denial output, version |
| Validation issue requiring a change to a user-visible contract | Stop at `repository validation`, send for formal review | Validation input, validation output, current revision |
| Same-named objects lack version identifiers | Suspend judgment | Object names, missing version identifiers, toolchain |

This table does not assign every issue to one person. The handoff recipient depends on the first verifiable boundary: maintainers of pkgs-release-automation continue investigating objects within the project, and issues go to the shared owner only after crossing a clearly defined interface. If the interface owner has not yet confirmed the input fields, just record that fact and do not fill in the fields on their behalf.

## Order for Collecting Incident Evidence

1. Save the first visible failure, including attachments, screenshots, or verbatim output.
2. Append the current entry point, version, and request/run id; mark each missing item as missing.
3. Mark the first difference, and do not place the last green rerun before the failure record.
4. Continue along only one branch: permissions, repository validation, environment differences, or entry point output.
5. Stop at a node where you reach an interface, fields are missing, or a contract change is required.

"Choose only one branch" is intended to prevent several guesses from being mixed into one result. Checking permissions and then changing the version, or switching environments and then cleaning up artifacts, will both make the next output no longer comparable. When the existing records are insufficient, stopping at the gap itself is more useful than filling in a seemingly complete attribution.

## Versions and Withdrawal

If the first current revision after the change fails, retain it even if later revisions pass. Rollback or withdrawal actions must also be recorded alongside the failure sample, rather than just writing "recovered". Before the exit action expires, retain at least the minimal input, version, and undo action; these materials are used to determine whether recovery occurred under the same conditions.

If recovery changed only the cache, permission identity, or entry point location, the result cannot be directly generalized to other conditions. Write the changed item next to the sample, then decide whether to compare again. This page only routes symptoms to the first clearly defined boundary and does not explain subsequent behavior for projects outside pkgs · Release Automation.

## Related Entry Points

IPDB-014 through IPDB-018 record, respectively, minimal input and undo actions, standard entry point denials, non-author review, the first revision after a change, and version identifier issues for same-named objects; they provide navigation to the corresponding incidents, not replacement records for this page. For the responsibility mapping, see DOC-37. title: Postmortem: Unmerged Compatibility Directory Records

versions.body:
# Postmortem: Unmerged Compatibility Directory Records

The initial anomaly was not a daemon startup failure, but that the compatibility directory had "current" records for two revisions at the same entry point. The entry point still appeared usable, but connection manager's record differed from the old record. At the time, it was unclear whether the directory update was lagging, the old record had not been moved out, or the two were describing different states to begin with.

Both records at the entry point were retained first, rather than continuing to overwrite one of them repeatedly. It was then confirmed that the IPC channel could still recover, and the user paths had not all failed immediately. As a result, the "inconsistency at the current entry point" was not recorded as daemon unavailability. This distinction mattered later: only one path that worked at the time had recovered; that did not mean the two records had been merged.

The on-call notes left three points unresolved:

- The revisions corresponding to the old and new records had not yet been checked individually;
- There was no evidence explaining why connection manager showed different results;
- The change in error identity had not yet been reproduced, so it could not be used to conclude that this was a daemon startup issue.

The original entry point is preserved at `docs/adj-daemon/incidents/daemon-compatibility-catalog-two-version-records-not-merged.md`. This version has no timestamp table because only the sequence of events had been confirmed at the time: first, two "current" results were observed; then, neighboring paths were found to still be usable; finally, further retries were stopped.

## Handling Decisions at the Time

The old entry was not deleted, and screenshots were not used in place of the entry point's contents. Keeping both records side by side would mislead consumers, but choosing one to overwrite the other would lose the revision clues needed for comparison. The incident's impact scope was provisionally recorded as "consumers that read the compatibility directory through the current entry point"; unconfirmed adopters were not included.

Details still to add: the last state before the failure that can be verified, and where each of the two records appeared.

# Postmortem: Unmerged Compatibility Directory Records

Two revisions in the compatibility directory once occupied the "current" entry at the same time. The earliest retained description only said that the connection manager differed from the old record; it did not say whether both records were actually read by real consumers. A later review found that the entry itself is not the same as the execution record: the page could show two same-named current results, with only one having an execution record.

That means v1's statement that "IPC channel can recover" is no longer enough to say the incident was over. Recovery of the IPC channel only proves that, at the time, one daemon lifecycle path did not stall; it does not tell us which directory record was selected or explain why the two current results coexisted.

## Sequence

| Stage | Confirmed facts | Action taken at the time |
|---|---|---|
| Initial observation | The current records for two revisions were at the same entry | Retained the entry contents without overwriting the old record |
| Investigation narrowed | The connection manager differed from the old record, but daemon startup could continue | Logged the directory anomaly separately from startup status |
| Comparison added | There were two same-named current results, and only one had an execution record | Stopped treating same names as the same result |
| Adjacent check | The adjacent item's current result was normal; the break occurred before the execution record | Focused verification on the path from the entry to the execution record |
| Recovery observed | One user path recovered | Left the root cause open |

This timeline does not add specific timestamps. The initial record did not preserve a reliable failure time; backfilling the time of the later review into the incident record would create false precision that did not exist.

## Impact

The affected consumers are those that use this entry to determine the "current revision." When the entry shows two records at once, a reader may treat the old record as the result still being used, or conversely overlook the one that still has an execution record. A normal adjacent item does not reduce this risk: it only shows that the adjacent item's entry-to-execution-record chain did not break at the same point.

There is no evidence that all daemon paths were affected. Daemon startup remained normal, so the failure was not recorded as a global startup interruption. There is also no evidence that the connection manager itself produced two directory records; it was simply the first place where the mismatch between the new and old records surfaced.

## Screenshot issue

IPDC-011 later pointed out that the screenshot of the current entry lacked provenance. The screenshot included no account, originating entry, or execution-record context, so it can serve only as corroborating evidence. The earlier wording that "the screenshot shows the current result" should be treated as too strong a claim: a screenshot can show that an interface displayed some content at some point, but it cannot show which record the content came from, much less that a consumer selected it.

For subsequent comparisons, use only the following sequence: first find the same-named records, then check whether each has an execution record, and only then verify the entry that reads it. Without the first two steps, do not use the screenshot to determine the old/new relationship.

```text
Current entry
  ├─ Current result A ── Has execution record
  └─ Current result B ── No execution record

Adjacent item ── Current result normal
```

A and B in the diagram are only labels for the two same-named results observed in the incident; they do not indicate version precedence. v1 treated "current" as a single location. This review corrects that: an entry may have more than one current result, and whether an execution record is present is a distinction that must be retained when comparing them.

## Adoption scope still unconfirmed

The verification task in IPDC-012 requires finding a real consumer that reads the current revision through the original entry and stops at the first difference. This requirement has not yet established the adoption scope. A normal adjacent item cannot substitute for the actual consumer's read result; it only provides a comparison point.

As of this version, we can say that the anomaly occurred between the current entry and the execution record, and that one adjacent normal record exists. We cannot say that both revisions were used, nor can we say that no one used the old record. Either possibility would lead to a different cleanup action, so the item without an execution record was not deleted from the directory.

## Failure at the ordinary entry

IPDC-017 added another phenomenon that needs to be kept separate: access by a non-admin identity to the ordinary entry for adj-daemon failed. This issue was not treated as part of the root cause of the two-revision record problem. Permission was denied while accessing the ordinary entry; the two-revision record problem occurred after the current result was read and before the execution record. They may appear in the same verification, but the available material does not establish a causal relationship.

When the ordinary entry fails, record the rejection point and the request/run id, then return to this record to compare the directory entries. If this context cannot be obtained, do not use the admin-view result as a substitute for the ordinary-entry result.

## Handling and outstanding items

The effective action in this review was to preserve the side-by-side state of the two revisions and separate "user path recovered" from "records merged." The ineffective actions were choosing one record as current based on a single screenshot and repeatedly retrying the entry without provenance.

Outstanding items:

- IPDC-006: the last confirmable state before failure;
- IPDC-011: which entry the screenshot came from and which account obtained it;
- IPDC-012: the first point of difference when a real consumer reads the current revision;
- IPDC-017: the ordinary-entry rejection point and its request/run id.

DOC-38 records a local note from the migration of the current entry to the old entry; this page preserves the anomalous sequence caused by the records for the two revisions not being merged. Both can help when revisiting the entry, but they should not substitute for each other.
