# Postmortem on Unmerged Compatibility Directory Records

The trouble left by this incident was not that old content had appeared in the directory, but that two revisions both appeared as "current" at the same entry point. The people who first checked saw a seemingly stable page: daemon startup did not stop immediately, and the IPC channel could still be restored; at the same time, however, what the connection manager saw differed from the old record. Looking at either side alone would lead to an overly simplistic conclusion.

Only later was it confirmed that current results with the same name do not amount to a single usable record. Only one of the two results had an execution record; although the other was at the current entry point, the available materials could not establish that it had actually been executed or adopted by consumers. This finding shifted the focus of the postmortem: the issue was no longer just "which revision is right", but that the entry point displayed records with different strengths of evidence side by side, making it easy for readers to mistake them for a single current state.

The initial notes, subsequent verification, and still-unfinished parts are retained below. They are arranged in the order of discovery, because "the path was restored", "the current entry point returned to normal", and "the old record was no longer in use" never referred to the same moment during this incident.

## Initial Observations

The assessment in v1 was narrow: the compatibility directory had placed the current records for two revisions at the same entry point; the connection manager's result differed from the old record; the IPC channel could still be restored. That version did not provide a complete timeline, nor did it include cards that only appeared later. It deliberately left two gaps: the revisions corresponding to the old and new records had not yet been checked individually, and the change in error identity had not yet been reproduced.

No further retries were made at the time, and neither record was deleted. This decision was not made because the old entry had been confirmed correct, but because deletion would destroy the most direct point of comparison. The simultaneous presence of two "current" results at the entry point was itself part of the observed state; choosing one as the sole current result first would only prevent later reviewers from knowing when and why the other had existed.

The statement in v1 that "user paths did not all stop working immediately" should also be read as originally intended. It was not a statement that all consumers were healthy, only that no complete halt of daemon startup had been observed at the scene. Expanding that sentence into "the directory issue had no impact" is incorrect: the directory entry point could still lead consumers to different revisions, and that risk would not be eliminated by a IPC channel that could still be restored.

The entry point retained at the time was:

`docs/adj-daemon/incidents/daemon-compatibility-catalog-two-version-records-not-merged.md`

It preserves the postmortem materials and attachment locations in incident-export. This path leads back to the compatibility directory records where the issue occurred, but it does not replace the execution record itself or provide the read results for all consumers.

## Earlier Assessment and Corrections

The early wording treated the "current entry point" as a single object. That framing was later overturned. The entry point can display two current results with the same name at once, but the evidence for the two results is not the same: one has an execution record, and the other does not.

> Deprecated working assumption: There is only one current result on the page, or results with the same name can be treated as equivalent based on their display position.

This assumption made manual comparison easier at the time, but it could not explain the differences observed later. If results with the same name are inherently equivalent, it cannot explain why adjacent entries are normal while this entry stops before the execution record; nor can it explain why one result is visible in the screenshot but its source and read context cannot be recovered.

The corrected wording is more restrained: the current entry point is a display location, not execution evidence. When comparing two revision entries, first confirm whether they have the same name, then confirm whether each has an execution record; without the second step, we cannot infer from "current" that something was "executed" or "adopted."

This does not attribute the issue to the directory implementation mechanism. Existing records do not prove who created the two results, nor do they prove that connection manager was responsible for merging or generating them. connection manager was the observation point where the discrepancy between the new and old records first became visible, not a confirmed root cause.

## Event timeline

| Order | Observed phenomenon | Conclusion that could be drawn at the time | Conclusion that could not be drawn from this |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | The current records for two revisions were located at the same entry point | The entry point can no longer be treated as the sole source of the current result | Cannot determine which one was adopted |
| 2 | connection manager differed from the old record | A visible discrepancy existed between the new and old records | Cannot determine that connection manager caused the discrepancy |
| 3 | daemon startup could still proceed, and the IPC channel could be restored | No global startup interruption was observed | Cannot determine that the directory anomaly had no impact |
| 4 | Of the two same-named current results, only one had an execution record | Same-named records must be compared separately | Cannot directly infer that something can be deleted from the absence of an execution record |
| 5 | The current result for the adjacent entry was normal | The chain from the adjacent entry point to the execution record did not have the same break | Cannot use the adjacent entry in place of verifying adoption for this entry |
| 6 | One user path was restored | That path worked again at the time | Cannot write this as though the two versions of the records had already been merged |
| 7 | A failure to access the ordinary entry point was reported | The context of the access denial needs to be recorded separately | Cannot fold the permission denial into the directory root cause |

The order in the table represents a change in understanding; it does not mean that all actions occurred within one continuous short time window. At the initial scene, no reliable, complete timestamp was available; the follow-up cards add verification tasks and observations and should not be retroactively written as though the incident timeline had already been known at the time.

## Why "recovery" did not end the incident

During the retrospective, the word most easily confused was "recovery." Here, there were at least three different situations:

1. daemon startup can continue;
2. the IPC channel is available again;
3. a particular user path works again.

On-site personnel may call all of these recovery, but none is sufficient to prove that the two versions of the records in the catalog have been merged. The first two describe availability at the daemon lifecycle level, while the third describes a single read path. Whether the catalog still displays two revisions, which entry has an execution record, and which entry actual consumers ultimately read are separate questions.

Therefore, this incident was not handled with a "close it as soon as it turns green" approach. What had worked was documenting the time of recovery separately from the time of root cause confirmation: after the user path was restored, both current results remained in scope for comparison; without records of actual use, the old entry was not removed, nor was the new entry documented as the sole authoritative one.

This also explains why v1 stopped at "stop further retries". Continuing to repeat daemon startup or IPC recovery would only verify the already known available paths again, without producing evidence that distinguishes the two catalog records. Subsequent work shifted to entry points, execution records and actual readers.

## Execution records become the dividing line

The subsequent review for IPDC-006 noted: there are two current results with the same name, and only one has an execution record. This fact is the strongest local distinction in this postmortem, not because an execution record automatically determines the correct revision, but because it makes "there is a current result on the page" and "that result has a traceable execution history" two distinguishable things.

Before this, on-site personnel had tended to interpret display position as priority. The problem with this approach is that the two entries already share the same entry point, and display position does not provide enough information to explain their relationship. Execution records at least provide a clear boundary for comparison: for an entry with a record, its execution process can be reviewed further; an entry without a record must be retained as a currently displayed entry of unknown origin, until its source is found or it is confirmed to be no longer in use.

This is still not a claim that "no execution record means it is wrong". The absence of an execution record may mean that the record was generated by a process that has not yet been located, or it may mean that the entry point has retained old output. The available material does not establish which of the two applies. Immediately cleaning it up as a junk entry would reintroduce the loss that v1 had avoided: the object of comparison is deleted first, and the cause cannot be traced later.

To keep subsequent verification from falling back on display position, the comparison order is fixed as follows:

```text
Current entry point
  │
  ├─ Find current results with the same name
  │      │
  │      ├─ With an execution record: continue investigating its execution process and read path
  │      └─ Without an execution record: retain the entry, find its source first, do not judge by page position
  │
  └─ Compare with adjacent normal entries
         └─ Use only to establish that this entry breaks before the execution record
```

This diagram is neither a remediation workflow nor a catalog implementation diagram. It only records the sequence of comparisons that has already emerged during this incident. Any approach that bypasses execution records and selects the "correct current" result directly from page screenshots will once again conflate two different levels of evidence.

## Limits of screenshots

IPDC-011 exposed another weakness: the screenshot of the current entry point lacks provenance. The screenshot does not identify the account used to obtain it, nor does it retain the entry-point context in which it was produced. It can prove that an interface once displayed certain content, but it cannot prove whether that content came from the result with an execution record or from another result with the same name.

It was inaccurate to describe the screenshot as "evidence of the current result" in the past. A more appropriate description is: the screenshot is supporting evidence that can help confirm that results were once displayed side by side; it cannot, on its own, establish the link between the revision, the execution record, and the actual consumers.

This distinction is also especially important for failures at the regular entry point. Results viewed as an administrator may bypass the point where the regular entry point denies access; even if the text in two screenshots is identical, this does not prove that a non-administrator can reach the same catalog state. If the screenshot's provenance is documented later, the account type, entry point, and whether it is possible to continue on to view the execution record should also be recorded. Without this context, the screenshot remains only supporting evidence.

## Why neighboring entries cannot stand in for this entry

The observation in IPDC-012 is: the current result for a neighboring entry is normal, while the break in this card occurs before the execution record. This provides a valuable comparison, but it does not answer who actually reads this entry.

A neighboring entry being normal means there is a nearby path in the same catalog that does not encounter the same break. It helps narrow the investigation from "all current results are broken" to the segment between this entry's entry point and its execution record. It cannot show that either of the two results with the same name has been adopted, much less that no one is using the old revision.

Previously, someone tried to use the neighboring entry's normal state as evidence that the catalog as a whole had recovered. This inference does not hold. The neighboring entry's name, record source, and readers cannot stand in for those of this entry; the comparison can only show that the difference lies near the point before the execution record, not transfer the outcome of another chain to this entry.

Verification with actual consumers still follows the method in IPDC-012: follow the original entry point to read the current revision, and stop at the first difference. Here, "stop at the first difference" is crucial. If someone first detours through another entry point or selects the entry with an execution record, then turns around and claims that the original entry point is normal, the comparison target has already been replaced, and the question initially raised by the incident cannot be answered.

As of this version, the extent of adoption by actual consumers remains undetermined. Therefore, this postmortem does not list the number of affected consumers, nor does it record the normal neighboring entry as evidence of recovery for this entry.

## Access failure at the regular entry point

The additional observation in IPDC-017 is adjacent to the issue involving the two revision records, but the two must not be conflated into a single root cause: accessing the normal entry point for adj-daemon as a non-admin fails. This card requires preserving the denial location and the request/run id. The existing materials do not provide either value, so this page does not invent them.

This failure may prevent actual consumers from completing verification through the original entry point, but it does not automatically explain why two revisions both became current results. The permission denial was observed while accessing the normal entry point; the anomaly involving the two revision records surfaced after entering the current results and before checking the execution records. Both need to be preserved because they affect the available paths in the same investigation; but without evidence linking them, neither can be described as the cause of the other.

When the normal entry point fails, a proper record of the situation should at least establish: whether the denial occurred before entering the catalog, while displaying the two current results, or when proceeding to inspect the execution records. Pinpointing this is more useful than "access failed" alone. If the context cannot be obtained as a non-admin, that gap should also be explicitly preserved rather than overwritten with a successful result from an admin page.

## Relationship to DOC-38

DOC-38 is a partial record left from the migration between the current and old entry points. It is connected to this incident because both involve the compatibility catalog entry point and old records; however, DOC-38 does not cover the incident sequence for this failure to merge the two revision records.

This page focuses on two revisions coexisting at the current entry point, asymmetric execution records, comparisons with adjacent entries, and blocked verification through the normal entry point. The migration note can help readers find context for the old entry point, but it cannot prove which consumer adopted the current entry. Conversely, the anomaly timeline on this page should not rewrite the migration context preserved in DOC-38.

Keeping the two documents side by side has practical value: one describes the partial traces left by the entry point migration, while the other explains why the same entry point could later no longer simply be treated as the single current state. Merging them into one record saying "the catalog has been cleaned up" would erase the uncertainty in the incident.

## Known Scope of Impact

At present, the confirmed scope of impact is very limited, but that does not mean there is no impact: readers who rely on the current entry point to determine the compatibility catalog revision may see two current results with the same name and be unable to tell from the page itself which one includes execution records. For these readers, the risk of error is not that the daemon will necessarily fail to start, but that they will use incomplete current-state markers to select records that should not be treated as equivalent.

The following situations have not been confirmed and are therefore not included in the scope of impact:

- All daemon lifecycle paths failed;
- All consumers read entries with no execution records;
- The connection manager wrote or merged directory records;
- Permission failures at the regular entry point caused two record versions to coexist;
- After the user path was restored, the two revisions had already been merged.

These are not minor differences in wording. If any one of them is treated as an established fact, subsequent cleanup will target the wrong thing: it might change the startup path, delete old records, or only fix access permissions, while overlooking the relationship between the entry point and the execution records that actually remains unverified.

## Benefits and drawbacks of the response actions

Three actions were retained.

First, the two records were kept side by side. This made it possible to confirm later that they had the same name but asymmetric execution records.

Second, daemon startup, the IPC channel and the directory adoption issue were kept separate. The fact that startup could still proceed did not obscure the entry-point issue, nor was the directory anomaly extrapolated into a global daemon failure.

Third, restoration of the user path was kept separate from root-cause confirmation. One restored path can be recorded as restored, but not used as a substitute for "merged".

Two actions also proved ineffective.

The first was relying on screenshots with no known source. The screenshots lacked account and entry-point context, so the page display could not be tied to a specific execution record.

The second was using normally functioning adjacent entries as a substitute for verifying this entry. Adjacent entries can only serve as breakpoint references, not represent actual consumers reading the current revision.

There is one more attempt that should explicitly be stopped: repeatedly accessing the same entry point without context. It cannot distinguish between permission denial, current results coexisting side by side and missing execution records, and instead adds "looks normal sometimes" noise. Subsequent access should start from the regular entry point, preserving the denial location for each identity; once access to the directory is possible, compare the records with the same name and the execution records.

## Questions still unanswered

1. What is the full revision corresponding to each of the two current records? The existing page descriptions are insufficient to establish a one-to-one mapping.
2. Which entry point or workflow produced the result with the same name but no execution record? The screenshots cannot answer this.
3. Did any actual consumer read an entry with no execution record through the original entry point? Verification for IPDC-012 has not yet established the scope of adoption.
4. At which stage of the regular entry-point flow does the denial occur? The denial location and request/run id are still missing for IPDC-017.
5. Is the change in error identity related to the issue with the two record versions? It was not reproduced in v1, and subsequent materials did not establish a connection either.

These questions are not empty fields awaiting polish; they are branch points that determine different handling paths. The first question determines whether the two records can be accurately traced back; the second and third questions determine whether the old entry should continue to be retained or can be safely processed; the fourth question determines whether verification by the actual user is blocked by access conditions; the fifth question determines whether the investigation needs to be extended to the daemon lifecycle side.

## Follow-up Verification Record Format

To avoid once again putting results from different levels into a single statement that says "currently normal," follow-up notes should record them separately:

| Object to verify | Content that must be retained | Non-substitutable content |
|---|---|---|
| Current entry | Whether the two same-named results are still listed side by side | The page location cannot substitute for the execution record |
| Execution record | Which one has an execution process | The presence or absence of an execution record alone cannot determine the adoption scope |
| Actual user | The first difference read through the original entry | A neighboring entry being normal cannot substitute for that read result |
| Ordinary entry | The rejection point and request/run id | An administrator-success page cannot substitute for the on-site observation through the ordinary entry |
| daemon lifecycle | The status of daemon startup and the IPC channel | Lifecycle availability cannot substitute for determining whether the directories were merged |

This is not a new operational checklist; it is a separation between records left by this incident. Any new material that can be clearly assigned to one of these rows can strengthen the comparison; if a description mixes the entry point, execution record, and adoption result, it should be split before being added.

## Current Assessment

As of this version, what has been confirmed is: the compatibility directory once placed the current records for two revisions under the same entry; of the two same-named current results, only one has an execution record; the current result of the neighboring entry is normal, while the break in this entry occurs before the execution record; there is also an independent observation that access through the ordinary entry fails for non-administrators.

What cannot currently be confirmed is: the complete origins of the two records, the adoption scope of the entry without an execution record, the causal relationship between the ordinary-entry failure and the coexistence of the two versions, and whether the change in error identity is related.

Therefore, the incident recovery assessment remains "one user path has been observed to recover" and is not upgraded to "the directory records have been merged." The old record continues to be retained; screenshots or the normal state of a neighboring entry must not be used in place of verification by the actual user through the original entry.

## Card Entry

IPDC-006 a supplemental record of the current entry-point state before the failure; IPDC-011 used to recover the entry point and account for the screenshots; IPDC-012 used to verify the first discrepancy when the actual consumer reads the current revision; IPDC-017 used to record the rejection point for the ordinary entry point and the request/run id. They correspond to different gaps in this postmortem and should not be merged into one generic "directory anomaly."

When adding materials next time, first state which unresolved question it answers, then preserve the uncertainty in the original situation. Only when the actual consumer's reading, the sources of the two records, and the relationship to the execution records can all be verified at the same time will it be possible to reassess whether the two versions of the records have truly been merged.

# release branch freeze Decision Record

The outcome of this freeze was a narrowed decision, not an exhaustive list of all configuration changes on the release branch. In the review, Northstar Desktop Systems focused the dispute on two adjacent actions: whether the current config-compatibility entry point should remain within the freeze scope, and whether the adjustment window should switch in the same round. The window itself was not rejected; the dispute was over whether it could be tied to the existing entry point as a single release action.

## The Choice Retained for Now

The review chose to retain the current entry point. Parts that can already be traced from the frozen repository through the exact runtime boundary can be included in the release branch freeze; parts where configuration topics are visible only in files or call names, but the runtime relationships have not yet been mapped out, are not included in this window change. The direct cost is that the old entry point remains, and the freeze was not used as an opportunity to complete the related adjustments at the same time.

The alternative was to combine the entry point adjustment with the window switch. Supporters of this proposal valued concentrating the changes so that another adjacent change would not need to be handled after the release. But at the time, there were not enough records to explain the compatibility cost between the existing entry point and the new window, nor had platform artifact identity been separated from changes in desktop behavior. The review therefore did not treat "the window is already due to switch" as a basis for combining the actions.

The meeting materials recorded two constraints at different levels:

> platform artifacts retain their image digest

and:

> Trace each desktop behavior from the frozen repository through the exact runtime boundary before changing it.

The first requires continuity in artifact identity during the freeze, while the second requires that the runtime boundary a behavior traverses can be explained before it is changed. Neither can be replaced by "the configuration name has already been found." Seeing only the entry point name does not establish that the adjustment window is already safe; likewise, retaining the same image digest does not, on its own, establish that desktop behavior has not changed because of an entry point change.

## Disagreement During the Review

At the time, one quicker reading was that as long as calls related to release, config, or platform could still be found in `src/tray.js`, that portion could be treated as existing evidence. Another reading required tracing further to the actual runtime boundary and confirming that the window switch did not create a gap between the location in the file and the behavior that would occur at release time. The latter criterion was adopted, but the review did not leave a complete record covering all callers.

As a result, "change first, trace back later" was not included in the decision. It appeared capable of avoiding one round of freeze coordination, but conflated three things that were not yet equivalent: the old entry point's compatibility status, the change to the adjustment window, and whether artifact identity would be maintained. Even if a successful outcome emerged later, the outcome alone could not be used to infer that all three had already been confirmed separately at the time of the freeze.

One objection raised at the time is retained here: the combined proposal might be cleaner, but it would carry unconfirmed compatibility costs past the freeze point. This objection did not mean the adjustment could never be made, nor did it grant the old entry point a long-term exemption; it only explains why a narrower scope was chosen for this round. If the window is reopened, the entry point change will need to be checked again against the runtime boundary and artifact identity separately.

## Freeze Relationships

The decision can be condensed into the following relationship from the review:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Retain the current config-compatibility entry point] --> B[Scope covered by existing evidence]
    B --> C[Include in release branch freeze]
    D[Include the adjustment window in the freeze] --> E[Compatibility costs not yet examined]
    E --> F[Defer this round]
```

"Defer" in the diagram refers to including the adjustment window in this round of the freeze, not rejecting the intended direction for the window. "Covered by existing evidence" in the diagram only means that the tracing criteria adopted for this review were met; it does not mean that all configuration call relationships have been fully mapped out.

## File Entry Point and Subsequent Recheck

This page originally used `src/tray.js` and related call names as starting points, and located areas associated with release, desktop, config, platform, image, and repository. This entry point can still help readers return to the local scope of the discussion: release information, desktop configuration, platform information, and artifact identity were all close to the dispute. But a file location is only a starting point for tracing; it must not be read as permanent ownership, nor can a stable location replace runtime boundary records.

An actual follow-up recheck was carried out later. The recheck again started from locations related to release, config, and platform in `src/tray.js`, then checked the call names to see whether they actually fell within this entry point discussion. It made the entry point easier to find, but did not produce new material sufficient to support "the adjustment window can be included directly." The recheck did not turn unconfirmed call relationships into definitive conclusions.

This recheck also preserved two judgments that are easily conflated. Artifacts can continue to meet the image digest requirement, but that is not evidence that entry point compatibility has been confirmed; conversely, finding the entry point's location is not proof of continuity in artifact identity. The freeze record separates the two precisely to prevent either from being used to validate the other.

## Earlier Proposals Rejected but Not Deleted

The old record still contains the judgment that "handling the adjustment window at the same time would be cleaner." It reflects the trade-off over release cadence at the time and was not later supported by new runtime records, so it remains in its historical context and must not be treated as a recommendation for the current entry point. Also retained is "change the entry point first, trace back later": it was once seen as a way to save on freeze coordination, but the review concluded that this sequence would make compatibility costs and artifact changes difficult to separate.

Neither proposal was implemented. They are recorded to explain why the freeze scope was narrowed, not to imply that a successful adjustment had ever been completed. If the issue is reopened later, at a minimum, runtime boundary records corresponding to the entry point change must be presented again, and the platform artifacts must be checked again to see whether they still meet the identity-retention requirements in the materials; this page does not specify a complete caller list or a replacement entry point name in advance for that recheck.

## Adjacent Handoff

The handoff for switching the Kubo packaging window remains in DOC-44. This page records only the release branch freeze decision on the config-compatibility entry point and does not bring in the packaging window steps. Both workstreams occurred during the same wrap-up phase, but they concern different objects, and the freeze judgment on one page cannot replace the handoff record on the other.

v2 adds the boundaries established by the actual recheck, rather than repackaging the record from an earlier point in time as current guidance. The final position still has three levels: the current entry point is retained this round; the scope already supported by tracing evidence can be frozen; the adjustment window and its compatibility cost in relation to the entry point have not been confirmed in this round. The last statement preserves the review's limitation without overturning the freeze decision already made.

# Code-reading notes: on-call rotation entry point

New teammates coming in through config-compatibility are likely to mistake it for a complete on-call guide. It isn't. The name only leads to the configuration compatibility layer; what actually needs tracing is where that one downstream call out of the configuration compatibility layer is first actually consumed by desktop on-call rotation.

The file opened along that path at the time was `src/daemon/config.js`. Pause at this file, but don't expand the review to all daemon configuration here, or add every file in the directory with config in its name to the reading list. Keep the tracing scope to a single direct caller. This isn't meant to prove that the files have no other relationships; it's meant to let whoever takes over retrace the route to the same rotation entry point.

```text
config-compatibility
        |
        v
src/daemon/config.js
        |
        |  one direct call
        v
first actual consumer of desktop on-call rotation
        |
        +-- edge that needs another owner to explain it: stop here
```

The route left in the first draft had an imprecise completion criterion: opening `config.js` was treated as having found the on-call entry point. That assessment was corrected during review. A file location only tells you where to continue reading; the entry point is connected to the rotation target only once you've followed that one direct call to the first actual consumer. Subsequent rotation arrangements, policy explanations, and handoff procedures aren't filled in along this path.

### Start at the entry point

Start with the public entry point of config-compatibility to confirm which compatibility object you're looking at. Record the entry point's name and its position on this path; there's no need to copy the entire configuration. Then go into `src/daemon/config.js` and look only for the direct call connected to that entry point. If a candidate is just a same-named definition, a mention in a comment, or part of adjacent compatibility logic without this call edge, don't treat it as the next stop.

Keeping the scope this narrow has a practical benefit: whoever takes over won't misread "configuration compatibility" as "the current rotation handles all desktop configuration." The two are close together when reading the code, but they aren't the same issue when on call. The first is a clue to the entry point; the second has no handoff target until the consumer appears.

### Follow the direct call only once

When following the direct call selected in `config.js` further down, don't fan out the search. The focused node run is used to check whether this one node takes the path into desktop on-call rotation; it's a navigation aid, not a reason to archive all related nodes together. If the run results show the call stopping inside configuration handling, stay at this layer to check; if it enters the rotation chain, just record the first consumer to receive that relationship.

"First" matters. Keep tracing and it's easy to run into notification, handoff, or other collaboration targets. They may also be related to on-call work, but they are no longer the entry point. Keeping the first consumer here lets later readers work backward from config-compatibility to confirm where the rotation picks up the configuration compatibility layer, rather than reconstruct the entire collaboration graph.

One working habit was added after the review: for each candidate, first ask whether it's called directly by the previous stop, then whether it already consumes rotation. The two questions must be answered in that order. If only the first is true, it may still be an intermediate forwarder; if only the second is true, it may come from another path. Only the two together identify the narrow path this tracing record is meant to retain.

### What to record when you get there

At the first actual consumer, three items are enough: the upstream entry point is still config-compatibility; the path passes through one direct call in `src/daemon/config.js`; and the consumer is the point where desktop on-call rotation first picks up that relationship. Don't write this up as long-term ownership, and don't infer from the filename who is responsible for every downstream issue.

Files with the same name but no call edge can still serve as signposts: they explain why someone might go off track, but shouldn't change the main route. Leave edges that need another owner to confirm them blank as well. That way, the next reader knows where to follow up, without treating unconfirmed policy-level relationships as established conclusions.

This review did not extend to other daemon startup paths. DOC-46 records a deviation in a different part of the release branch freeze; it can't be used to fill in the call relationships here.

# Release Freeze Window Discrepancy Postmortem

During the release branch freeze window, the final visible result did not settle as originally planned. At the first check, one record still treated the candidate content as a result ready to freeze, while a cross-process event record did not line up with that result. The window did not proceed on the basis of the original confirmation assessment.

## Shift Timeline

At first, this was tentatively recorded as a display discrepancy on the release branch. That assessment described what was visible at the time but did not explain why the cross-process events were split. The retained cross-process event trace did not identify a clear point of loss either.

Freeze confirmation based on a single visible result was then paused in favor of checking both the artifacts and event records. This allowed work in the window to continue but did not establish whether the discrepancy came from the branch, the build process, or event delivery. The original "just a display issue" note was kept in the record; it represented the shift's working hypothesis, not a verified cause.

## Impact and Recovery

The confirmed impact was on the freeze assessment for this window. When the visible result differed from the original plan, manual confirmation based on that result no longer had a valid basis. The available material does not show that the same discrepancy spread to other windows, nor does it support classifying it as a single-platform issue.

After temporary recovery, a control was added: platform artifacts retain their image digest. Retaining an image digest for comparison during the window can avoid being left with only a release view that cannot be revisited once status messages change. This control reduces ambiguity for the next check, but it cannot replace an investigation into event ordering and does not mean the root cause has been identified.

## Unknowns

It is still unclear where the discrepancy first arose: the pre-freeze candidate assessment, inter-process event delivery, or the timing of artifact presentation. The existing trace only shows that the records did not line up. The recovery action improved the confirmation path, but the cause cannot be inferred from it; follow-up reviews still need to compare the artifacts, original plan, and event order in a single record.
